title: Magnets and magnetic materials: the magnet pulls the nail, but does the nail pull back?

summary.text: A magnet picks up a nail, so it looks as if the magnet does all the pulling. But float the magnet on a tiny raft, hold a nail near it, and the magnet sails across the water to the nail. Your child tests this with two rafts, finds out why two nails hanging from one magnet spread apart in a V, and tests how well nails, needles and fridge magnets keep their magnetism. Along the way they meet soft iron, hard steel, keepers (pieces of iron that help a stored magnet stay strong), and a rule about pulls: they always come in pairs.
summary.art: A plastic tub of water with two small rafts, one carrying a round magnet and one carrying a steel nail, both drifting towards each other with small arrows.

intro.hook: A magnet can pick up a nail. Everyone says the magnet is pulling the nail. But what if the nail is pulling the magnet too? Put the magnet on a little boat on water and bring a nail close. What do you think the boat will do?
intro.text: In Class 3 you found out that a magnet attracts iron, and that every iron atom is a tiny magnet. Now we go one step deeper. How does a plain nail, which is not a magnet, get pulled at all? Why do two nails hanging from one magnet spread apart? Why does a needle stay magnetic when a nail does not? And how can a fridge magnet grip your almirah on one side only? You find out by testing it yourself.
intro.art: A child's hand holding a steel nail close to a small foam raft on water, with a round magnet on the raft turning towards the nail.

outcomes: I can explain that when a magnet attracts a nail, the nail attracts the magnet just as strongly, and I can show it with floating rafts.
I can explain why the lighter of two things pulled together moves further, even though the two pulls are equal.
I can explain that a nail near a magnet becomes a temporary magnet itself, and use this to explain why two hanging nails spread apart.
I can use a repel test to tell a real magnet from a plain piece of iron.
I can explain the difference between soft magnetic materials, which lose their magnetism, and hard ones, which keep it, and say which jobs each is used for.
I can explain why magnets are stored with keepers, and what weakens a magnet.
I can say how a fridge magnet, a hard disk and a magnetic stripe use many tiny magnetised regions.
I can say what scientists agree on about a magnetic field, and what they still argue about.

terms.meaning: The force between a magnet and a magnetic material, or between two magnets. It can attract or repel, and it acts across a gap.
terms.example: A magnet held just above a pin pulls the pin up before they touch.
terms.art: A magnet above a steel pin with the pin leaping up towards it.

terms.meaning: To pull towards. Two things attract each other when the force between them pulls them together.
terms.example: A magnet and a nail attract each other.
terms.art: A magnet and a nail with two arrows pointing towards each other.

terms.meaning: To push away. Only a magnet can repel another magnet. A plain piece of iron is never pushed away.
terms.example: Turn one fridge magnet round and it pushes the other one away.
terms.art: Two round magnets with arrows pointing away from each other.

terms.meaning: A material that a magnet attracts, such as iron, most steel, nickel and cobalt. It is not a magnet by itself.
terms.example: A steel nail is a magnetic material. It is not a magnet until a magnet is near.
terms.art: A steel nail lying beside a bar magnet.

terms.meaning: A magnet that keeps its magnetism for years without anything to help it.
terms.example: A fridge magnet and a bar magnet are permanent magnets.
terms.art: A bar magnet holding a chain of paper clips on a shelf.

terms.meaning: A piece of magnetic material that acts as a magnet only while a magnet is near it.
terms.example: A nail hanging from a magnet can hold a pin. Pull the magnet away and the pin drops.
terms.art: A nail hanging from a magnet holding a pin, and the same nail alone with the pin on the table.

terms.meaning: A magnet that a nearby magnet has made in a piece of magnetic material. The word induced means brought about by something else.
terms.example: The nail that hangs from a magnet and holds up a paper clip is an induced magnet.
terms.art: A magnet, a nail below it and a clip below the nail, with small arrows inside the nail.

terms.meaning: A magnetic material that is easy to magnetise and loses its magnetism quickly. Soft here does not mean squashy. It is only about magnetism.
terms.example: A plain iron nail is a soft magnetic material.
terms.art: A plain iron nail with a few clips falling from it.

terms.meaning: A magnetic material that is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism for a long time. Hard here is also only about magnetism.
terms.example: A steel sewing needle is a hard magnetic material.
terms.art: A steel needle holding a pin.

terms.meaning: To take the magnetism out of a magnet. Heat, hard knocks and a strong opposite magnet can all do it.
terms.example: Hammering a magnet hard many times makes it weaker.
terms.art: A hammer above a bar magnet and a small crack mark.

terms.meaning: A piece of soft iron laid across the ends of a magnet when it is stored, to help it keep its magnetism.
terms.example: A horseshoe magnet in a shop is often stored with a flat iron bar across its two ends.
terms.art: A horseshoe magnet with a flat iron bar across its two ends.

terms.meaning: An end of a magnet where its pull is strongest. There is a north pole and a south pole.
terms.example: Paper clips cling to the two ends of a bar magnet.
terms.art: A bar magnet with clips clinging to both ends.

terms.meaning: A tiny region inside iron or steel where the tiny magnets of billions of atoms point the same way.
terms.example: In a plain nail the domains point different ways, so the nail is not a magnet.
terms.art: A zoomed-in nail with small patches, each with an arrow pointing a different way.

terms.meaning: The point when all the domains in a piece of iron already point the same way, so no magnet can make it any more magnetic.
terms.example: A thin nail can be magnetised only up to a limit, however strong the magnet.
terms.art: A nail with all its small arrows pointing the same way.

terms.meaning: How much stuff something is made of. A heavier thing has more mass. We measure mass in grams and kilograms.
terms.example: A steel spoon has more mass than a plastic spoon of the same size.
terms.art: A kitchen scale showing a steel spoon and a plastic spoon.

terms.meaning: Isaac Newton's rule that when one thing pushes or pulls another, the other pushes or pulls back just as hard, in the opposite direction.
terms.example: When you push a wall, the wall pushes your hand.
terms.art: A girl pushing a wall with her palm and a matching arrow coming back from the wall.

terms.meaning: A hard dark ceramic made from iron oxide, which is iron joined with oxygen. Most fridge magnets and speaker magnets are made of ferrite.
terms.example: The black round magnet inside an old loudspeaker is ferrite.
terms.art: A black round ceramic magnet next to a loudspeaker.

terms.meaning: A very strong small magnet made from neodymium, iron and boron. It is much stronger than a ferrite magnet of the same size.
terms.example: Tiny silver magnets inside earphones and phones are neodymium magnets.
terms.art: A tiny silver magnet lifting a heavy steel bolt.

terms.meaning: A thin band on a card that holds information as many tiny regions magnetised one way or the other.
terms.example: The dark stripe on an old bank card or a hotel key card is a magnetic stripe.
terms.art: An old bank card with a dark stripe along the back.

explanations.concept: A pull has two ends: the nail pulls the magnet too
explanations.definition: When a magnet attracts a nail, the nail attracts the magnet with exactly the same strength, in the opposite direction. The two pulls always come as a pair.
explanations.description: We say 'the magnet pulls the nail' because the nail is the one we see move. But float the magnet on water, hold the nail still, and the magnet moves to the nail. The nail was pulling all along. Isaac Newton wrote this as a rule in his book of 1687, the Principia. It is called the third law of motion. When one thing pushes or pulls another, the other pushes or pulls back, equally hard. You feel it every day. Push a wall and you feel the wall push your hand. Stand on skates and push a wall, and you roll backwards. The wall did not move, but it pushed you.
examples: A magnet on a raft sails to a held nail, so the nail is pulling the magnet.
A swimmer pushes the water back, and the water pushes the swimmer forward.
A falling apple pulls the Earth upwards by exactly as much as the Earth pulls the apple down. The Earth is so heavy that it moves by a tiny amount that we can never see.
explanations.art: A magnet on a raft and a nail on another raft, with one equal arrow on each pointing towards the other.

explanations.concept: Equal pulls do not mean equal moves
explanations.definition: Two things pulled together by equal forces move different distances if they have different mass. The one with less mass moves more.
explanations.description: Push a light shopping bag and a heavy school bag with the same push. The light one slides far, and the heavy one hardly moves. It is the same with a magnet and a nail. The two pulls are equal. If both float on rafts that have the same mass, they meet in the middle. If the nail raft is three times heavier, it moves a third as far, and the magnet raft does most of the travelling. This is why a fridge magnet seems to do all the work when it jumps onto an almirah. The almirah is pulled just as hard. It has so much mass, and so much friction with the floor, that it does not move.
examples: A tiny magnet jumps to a heavy iron pan, and the pan does not move. The pan is pulling the magnet with exactly the same force.
Two rafts of equal mass, one with a magnet and one with a nail, meet in the middle of the tub.
If you hold a magnet in your hand and a pin hangs from a thread, the pin swings to the magnet. The magnet pulls your hand too, but your hand is far too heavy to feel it.
explanations.art: Two rafts, one tiny and one big, joined by equal arrows, with the tiny raft far from its start and the big raft hardly moved.

explanations.concept: A nail near a magnet becomes a magnet itself
explanations.definition: A piece of iron near a magnet becomes an induced magnet. The magnet turns the domains inside the iron to point one way, and the iron becomes a magnet for as long as the magnet stays near.
explanations.description: Why does a magnet pick up a plain nail at all? A plain nail is not a magnet. Its domains point in all directions and cancel out. When a magnet comes near, its magnetic field turns the domains in the nail to point the same way. Now the nail is a magnet too, with its own north and south poles. The end of the nail closest to the magnet's north pole becomes a south pole, and a north pole and a south pole attract. So a magnet never attracts plain iron directly. It first makes the iron into a magnet, and then the two magnets attract each other. This is also why a chain of clips can hang from a magnet. Each clip becomes a magnet and holds the next one.
examples: A nail touching a magnet can pick up pins. Pull the magnet away and most pins fall.
Either end of a plain iron nail pulls a compass needle. The needle is a small magnet, so it makes the nail into a magnet, and the two attract.
A chain of paper clips hangs from one magnet, with every clip magnetised by the one above.
explanations.art: A magnet, a nail and a clip in a column, with small arrows inside the nail and the clip all pointing the same way.

explanations.concept: Why two hanging nails spread apart like a V
explanations.definition: Two nails hanging from the same pole of a magnet spread apart because both become magnets with the same kind of pole at their free ends, and two poles of the same kind repel.
explanations.description: Touch the heads of two nails to the north pole of a magnet. Each nail becomes an induced magnet. The head, next to the magnet's north pole, becomes a south pole. The far end, the tip, must then be a north pole. Both tips are north poles, and two north poles repel. So the tips push each other apart, and the two nails hang in a V. If you use the magnet's south pole instead, the same thing happens, and both tips are south poles. The longer the nails are, the further their tips are from the magnet and from each other, so they have more room to spread.
examples: Two pins hanging from one magnet spread at the tips.
Three pins hang as a small bunch, with the tips pushing apart as far as they can.
Clips hanging one below the other in a chain hang in a straight line. Each clip has only one clip below it, and no clip beside it to push away.
explanations.art: A magnet at the top with two nails hanging from it in a V shape, and the same pole letter marked on each tip.

explanations.concept: Only a magnet can repel: the repel test
explanations.definition: If two things attract each other, you cannot tell if one is a magnet or both are. If two things repel, both must be magnets. Repelling is the proof of a magnet.
explanations.description: A plain nail is attracted by either end of a magnet. A magnet is attracted by one end of another magnet and pushed away by the other end. So here is a test for a mystery piece of metal. Float a magnet on a raft, or hang it from a thread. Bring one end of the mystery piece near, then the other end. If either end pushes the magnet away, the mystery piece is a magnet. If both ends pull, it is plain iron, or a magnet that is too weak to push. A pull can come from a magnet or from plain iron, but a push can only come from a magnet. That is why scientists treat a repulsion as stronger evidence than an attraction.
examples: A stroked needle pushes the floating magnet away with one end, so it really is a magnet.
A plain nail pulls the floating magnet with both ends, so it is only magnetic.
A fridge door pulls a fridge magnet, but it never pushes the magnet away, so the door is not a magnet.
explanations.art: A floating magnet with one end of a needle pushing it away, and a plain nail pulling it from both ends.

explanations.definition: A soft magnetic material, such as plain iron, is easy to magnetise and loses its magnetism as soon as the magnet goes away. A hard magnetic material, such as hard steel, is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism for years.
explanations.description: Touch an iron nail and a steel sewing needle to a magnet, and both pick up pins. Take the magnet away. The nail drops most of its pins. The needle keeps its pins, and it can still lift a pin next week. Scientists call the nail soft and the needle hard. These words mean something different from 'soft' and 'hard' in a toy shop. They only describe how easily the domains turn and how well they stay turned. The two kinds are used for different jobs. A permanent magnet is made from a hard material, so it keeps its magnetism. The core of an electromagnet, a coil of wire with electricity running through it, is made from a soft material. When the electricity is switched off, the core stops being a magnet. That is how a scrapyard crane drops its load.
examples: Fridge magnets, loudspeaker magnets and compass needles are made of hard magnetic materials.
The iron core inside an electric bell or a scrapyard crane magnet is a soft magnetic material.
A screwdriver can become a little magnetic after it is stroked with a magnet, because its steel is fairly hard.
explanations.art: A needle holding pins after the magnet has gone, next to a plain nail with its pins fallen on the table.

explanations.concept: Why hard steel keeps its magnetism
explanations.definition: Hard steel keeps its magnetism because tiny flaws and bits of carbon in the steel hold its domains in place after they have turned.
explanations.description: In pure soft iron, the edge between one domain and the next can slide about easily, so the domains turn back by themselves once the magnet leaves. In hard steel, there are tiny bits of carbon and other flaws in the way. They act like pebbles in a stream, and the domain edges catch on them. Once the domains are turned, they stay turned. This is why adding carbon to iron to make steel changes its magnetism as well as its strength. It is also why hammering, heating or a strong opposite magnet can undo the magnetism of a needle. They shake the edges loose from the flaws. Scientists know this from studying domains under special microscopes.
examples: A sewing needle has a lot of carbon, so it stays magnetised.
Alnico, a mixture of aluminium, nickel, cobalt and iron, is built so that its domains are held very firmly.
A magnet that is hammered hard many times gets weaker.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in view of a domain edge catching on small dots inside steel, and sliding freely inside plain iron.

explanations.definition: When a magnet slowly magnetises a piece of iron, the domains do not turn smoothly. They flip in sudden small jumps, and the jumps can be heard as a crackle. This is called the Barkhausen effect.
explanations.description: In 1919, the German physicist Heinrich Barkhausen wound a coil of wire around an iron rod. He joined the coil to a new kind of amplifier and a loudspeaker. Then he moved a magnet slowly towards the rod. The loudspeaker crackled like oil frying. Each click was a group of domains turning over all at once. So iron does not become a magnet smoothly, the way a dimmer switch slowly brightens a light. It changes in thousands of tiny jumps, like a crowd standing up one row at a time. Engineers today use the same crackle to test steel parts, because a part with a hidden flaw crackles in a different way.
examples: Slowly bringing a magnet near an iron rod makes a loudspeaker crackle.
Engineers listen to the crackle of a steel gear to find out if it was heated properly.
The crackle is like rain on a tin roof. Each click is one drop, and there are thousands.
explanations.art: A magnet moving towards an iron rod wound with wire, connected to a loudspeaker with small crackle marks.

explanations.concept: A piece of iron can only be magnetised so far
explanations.definition: When every domain in a piece of iron already points the same way, the iron is saturated. Even a stronger magnet cannot make it any more magnetic.
explanations.description: The more a magnet turns the domains in a nail, the stronger the nail's own magnetism gets. But there is a limit. A thin nail has only so many domains to turn. Once they all point the same way, that is the most magnetism the nail can ever have. A fat bolt has many more domains, so it can hold a stronger magnetism. This is why a thin sheet of tin, held on a fridge magnet, grips less than a thick plate of the same steel. It is also why engineers who make strong electromagnets choose a fat iron core. Once the iron is saturated, a stronger magnet changes almost nothing.
examples: A thick bolt can lift more pins than a thin nail, when both touch the same magnet.
However strong the magnet, a thin steel wire cannot become a stronger magnet than its saturation limit allows.
A cup holds only so much water. After it is full, a stronger tap adds nothing.
explanations.art: A thin nail and a fat bolt, each with small arrows inside, with the fat bolt holding more clips.

explanations.concept: Keepers: why magnets are stored in pairs
explanations.definition: A keeper is a piece of soft iron laid across the poles of a magnet. It gives the magnet's field an easy path from one pole to the other, and helps the magnet to stay strong.
explanations.description: A bar magnet works slightly against itself. Its own north pole sits not far from its own south pole, and the field from one pole tends to turn the domains near the other pole backwards. Over many years, this can make the magnet weaker. A keeper is a small bar of soft iron. When it lies across the poles, the field runs through the iron instead of around through the air, and the magnet's domains are not pushed backwards. Shops once kept horseshoe magnets with a flat iron bar across their ends. Two bar magnets stored side by side with opposite poles together, and a keeper at each end, hold in the field in the same way. The magnets that need this most are made from materials like alnico. Modern ferrite and neodymium magnets keep their magnetism far better and need less care.
examples: A horseshoe magnet with a flat iron bar across its ends.
Two bar magnets stored in a box side by side, north next to south, with an iron bar across each end.
Store fridge magnets stacked with their sticking faces together, not loose in a drawer with metal tools.
explanations.art: A box with two bar magnets lying side by side with opposite poles together and a small iron bar across each end.

explanations.concept: A fridge magnet that grips on one side only
explanations.definition: A bendy fridge magnet is rubber filled with ferrite powder, magnetised in many thin stripes of north and south side by side. This makes it grip strongly on one face and hardly at all on the other.
explanations.description: Try this with a flat bendy fridge magnet. Press its front on the steel door, and it holds well. Flip it over, and it barely sticks. The two faces are different. The maker magnetises the rubber sheet in thin stripes: a north pole, then a south pole, then a north pole again. The field loops between the neighbouring stripes. On the front face, the loops reach out far enough to grip steel. On the back, the loops cancel out and the grip is weak. The stripes are only about a millimetre or two wide, so your fingers do not notice them, but a special viewing film shows them. This is good design: the magnet's pull is put on the one face that needs it.
examples: A bendy fridge magnet sticks to the fridge on one side only.
The rubber strip that seals a fridge door has a magnetic strip inside it, so the door pulls itself shut.
Cut a bendy fridge magnet in two with scissors, and each piece is still a magnet, with its own strong side.
explanations.art: A bendy fridge magnet seen from the side, with alternating north and south stripes and curved loops reaching out of the front face only.

explanations.definition: A small magnet can lift a nail up against the pull of the whole Earth. This shows that the magnetic force is much stronger than gravity between everyday things.
explanations.description: The whole Earth is pulling the nail down. It has an enormous mass. A small ceramic magnet, which you can hold in your fingers, pulls the nail up and wins. Scientists have compared the strengths of the forces of nature. Gravity is by far the weakest of them. Gravity only seems strong because the Earth is so huge. Gravity never pushes, it only pulls, so the pull of every bit of the Earth adds up. The magnetic force is a part of the electromagnetic force, which also holds atoms together. It is much stronger than gravity between two small things. A fridge magnet beats the Earth in a tug of war, but only at a gap of a few millimetres. It loses its grip quickly as the gap grows.
examples: A small magnet holds a nail against the Earth's pull.
A paper clip hangs from a magnet, and a whole planet cannot pull it off.
Drop a nail and gravity pulls it to the floor. Hold a small magnet just above it and the magnet lifts it back up.
explanations.art: A small magnet holding up a nail, and a large Earth below with a thin arrow pulling the nail down.

explanations.concept: Magnetic pull and static pull are not the same
explanations.definition: A magnet pulls only iron, nickel, cobalt and a few other materials. A rubbed comb pulls scraps of paper. These are two different pulls, and a simple test tells them apart.
explanations.description: Rub a plastic comb on dry hair, and it picks up tiny bits of paper. Is the comb a magnet? Test it. A magnet does not pick up bits of paper, and a rubbed comb does not pick up a steel pin. The comb's pull is static electricity, which comes from electric charge. The magnet's pull is magnetism. Scientists have found that electricity and magnetism are two sides of one force, the electromagnetic force. James Clerk Maxwell wrote the rules for it in 1865. But in the kitchen, they behave differently, and the tests show which one you have. This is what a scientist does first: test what picks up what.
examples: A rubbed comb picks up paper but not a pin.
A magnet picks up a pin but not paper.
A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall, and a magnet does not stick to a plastered wall.
explanations.art: A comb picking up paper scraps on the left and a magnet picking up pins on the right.

explanations.concept: Magnetic memory: how a hard disk and a card hold information
explanations.definition: A magnetic stripe, a cassette tape and a hard disk store information as millions of tiny regions of magnetic material, each magnetised one way or the other. Each region is like a domain that has been turned on purpose.
explanations.description: A hard disk has a thin coat of hard magnetic material on a spinning plate. A tiny coil called a write head passes over it and turns each tiny region of the coat either up or down. A pattern of ups and downs can stand for numbers, and the numbers can stand for letters, pictures and sound. To read it back, a tiny sensor called a read head passes over the plate and feels which way each region points. This only works because the material is hard. The regions must stay turned for years, or the information would fade. Old cassette tapes and the dark stripe on an old bank card work in the same way. Strong magnets near them can scramble the pattern, which is why you are told to keep cards away from magnets.
examples: A hotel key card or an old bank card has a dark magnetic stripe.
An old cassette tape is a thin ribbon coated with magnetic powder.
A hard disk inside a computer stores a whole library on spinning magnetic plates.
explanations.art: A spinning disk with tiny arrows pointing up and down along a track, and a small head above it.

explanations.concept: Is a magnetic field a real thing?
explanations.description: A magnet moves a nail across a gap with nothing in between. How does the pull cross the gap? Scientists use the idea of a magnetic field, a map of the pull at every place around the magnet. They agree the field works as a description. They do not all agree what it is.
examples: Iron filings sprinkled on paper over a magnet line up along the field.
A compass held in a magnetic field turns to point along it.
Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields moving through space, and it can cross empty space.

perspectives.explanation: In a letter, Newton said it was absurd that one body could act on another across empty space with nothing between them. He did not offer an answer.
Faraday, a self-taught scientist who began work as a bookseller's boy, pictured lines of force filling the space around a magnet. He said the lines are real.
The field is real, because it carries energy and light is a wave of it. Fields cross empty space. The exact nature of the field, and how it connects to quantum physics, is still being worked out.
The field is a very good description, but we only ever measure the pulls. Asking whether the field is a thing is a question science cannot settle by measuring.

explanations.art: Iron filings in curved lines around a magnet, with four small speech bubbles from four different thinkers.

agreed.text: A magnet and a piece of iron pull each other with exactly equal force, in opposite directions.
agreed.evidence: Newton's third law has been tested for over 300 years. Floating rafts show it: a magnet on one raft and a nail on the other both move.

agreed.text: A piece of plain iron near a magnet becomes a magnet itself for as long as the magnet is near.
agreed.evidence: The nail picks up pins while it touches the magnet, and drops them when the magnet goes. Special microscopes show the domains turning.

agreed.text: Soft magnetic materials lose their magnetism quickly, and hard ones keep it.
agreed.evidence: A nail drops its pins, and a needle keeps them. Engineers use the two kinds for different jobs.

agreed.text: Only a magnet can repel another magnet.
agreed.evidence: Plain iron is attracted by both ends of a magnet. A push away has only ever been seen between two magnets.

agreed.text: Magnets can be weakened by heat, hard knocks and strong opposite magnets.
agreed.evidence: People have measured the loss of strength in hammered and heated magnets for centuries.

agreed.text: Magnetic stripes, tapes and disks store information as many tiny regions magnetised one way or the other.
agreed.evidence: Engineers write and read the patterns every day, and magnetic viewers show them.

challenging.claim: The magnet does all the pulling. The nail is just pulled.
challenging.for: The nail is the one that moves, and the magnet stays in your hand.
challenging.against: Float the magnet on a raft and hold the nail, and the magnet moves instead. The two pulls are always equal. Which one moves depends on which one is free to move and how heavy it is.

challenging.claim: A magnet holds a nail the way glue or suction does.
challenging.for: The nail sticks and does not fall.
challenging.against: A magnet pulls through air and paper, with a gap, and it works in empty space. Glue needs touching, and suction needs air. A magnet needs neither.

challenging.claim: If two things attract, one of them must be a magnet.
challenging.for: A magnet and a nail attract, and a magnet is one of them.
challenging.against: Two plain iron nails near a magnet attract each other, and neither was a magnet before. Even when one magnet pulls a plain nail, two magnets are pulling, because the magnet has made the nail into a magnet. Only a push proves that a thing is a magnet by itself.

challenging.claim: A magnet loses strength every time it lifts something, like a battery running down.
challenging.for: Old magnets are often weaker than new ones.
challenging.against: Holding a nail for years takes nothing from a magnet. Old magnets weaken because of heat, knocks, nearby opposite magnets or very slow changes inside the material. A good magnet can hold a weight for decades.

challenging.claim: A stronger magnet always lifts a heavier load.
challenging.for: Strong magnets do lift heavy things.
challenging.against: What the magnet lifts also matters. A thin sheet of steel saturates early and gives the magnet less to hold. A rough, rusty or curved surface leaves tiny gaps. A flat thick plate lets the same magnet hold much more.

challenging.claim: Every magnet must have iron in it.
challenging.for: Most everyday magnets have iron, and the old magnet stone was made of iron oxide.
challenging.against: A samarium-cobalt magnet, in its simplest form, is made of only samarium and cobalt, with no iron. What matters is whether the atoms line up in domains.

challenging.claim: A magnetic field is only a drawing and not a real thing.
challenging.for: We only ever measure the pulls on things.
challenging.against: A field carries energy, and light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields travelling through empty space. Most physicists say this makes fields real.

big_questions.q: The magnet pulls the nail, and the nail pulls the magnet. When we say 'the magnet pulls the nail', are we telling the story from the nail's side or from the magnet's?
big_questions.hint: Is there a way to describe the pair without picking a side?

big_questions.q: A pull needs two things. Can anything act on the world without the world acting back on it?
big_questions.hint: Think about walking, speaking, planting a seed.

big_questions.q: A nail becomes a magnet the moment a magnet is near and stops when it goes. Is the nail 'really' a magnet or 'really' not?
big_questions.hint: Does a word like 'magnet' describe a thing or what is happening to it?

big_questions.q: A needle keeps its magnetism for years, and a nail forgets in seconds. What do you think it means for a material to 'remember'?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to find out to say a material remembers?

big_questions.q: The magnetic force beats the whole Earth's gravity, yet we say gravity is the force that holds the universe together. How can the weaker force be the one that shapes planets and stars?
big_questions.hint: Think about what adds up over a huge amount of stuff, and what cancels.

big_questions.q: The same domains that make a fridge magnet also store the songs on a hard disk. Does knowing that a song is held by tiny magnetised regions change how you feel about the music?
big_questions.hint: Are you still the same you if you know what your brain is made of?

big_questions.q: Two people who work together to move a heavy thing both move it, but only one might get the thanks. Who does the 'pulling' in a team?
big_questions.hint: Who is the nail, and who is the magnet?

big_questions.q: Newton thought it was absurd that one thing could pull another across empty space. Faraday, who had no university education, found a way to picture it. Why do you think a new way of seeing sometimes comes from outside the usual path?
big_questions.hint: Who was allowed to study science in the 1800s, and who was not?

big_questions.q: We feel sure the magnet is the one pulling, because the nail is the one that moves. What other times in life do we think one side is the 'doer' because the other side is the one that moves?
big_questions.hint: Think about a river and its bank, a teacher and a class, a mother and a baby.

big_questions.q: A repulsion is stronger proof of a magnet than an attraction. What other kinds of evidence are stronger when they say 'no' than when they say 'yes'?
big_questions.hint: Think about a fever test, or a lock that does not open.

story.title: The Train That Met in the Middle
story.note: A made-up story. Channapatna in Karnataka really is known as the toy town, and its wooden toys are coloured with lac while the wood spins on a lathe. Revathi, her family and the toy buyer are made up. The science is real: when a magnet and a nail pull each other, the pulls are equal, and the lighter one moves more.
text: In the town of Channapatna, where the streets smell of wood shavings and warm lac, ten-year-old Revathi lived in a house full of toys. There were wooden tops on the shelves, wooden rattles hanging from the beams, and wooden elephants lined up on the windowsill, all in shiny red and yellow and green.

Her Ajji, her grandmother, turned the wood on a lathe. The wood spun and spun, and Ajji pressed a stick of coloured lac against it. The lac softened in the heat of the spinning and spread over the wood like a ribbon of butter. Ajji never looked at her hands. She looked at the wood, and the wood told her what to do.

One morning, a woman came to the house on a red scooter. Her name was Mrs Nasreen Khan, and she owned a toy shop in Hyderabad. She put a small wooden train on the table. It had an engine and two carriages, joined by tiny metal hooks.

'The children love it,' she said. 'But the hooks catch little fingers, and the mothers complain. Can you make me a train whose carriages join without hooks? No pinching, no hooks. They should simply find each other.'
Revathi's mind lit up. She had a ceramic magnet from the back of an old loudspeaker. 'Ajji, I can do it with a magnet!'

She hid the magnet in the back of the engine, and a steel nail in the front of each carriage. She placed the engine on the table with a carriage a hand's width behind it. The carriage rolled forward, all on its own, and joined the engine with a click.

'Wonderful,' said Mrs Khan. But Revathi's uncle Mohan, who painted the faces on the elephants, frowned. 'It is not good enough yet. Look, the engine has the magnet. The magnet is the one doing the pulling. The nail is only being pulled, like a fish on a line. If we want a stronger join, we will use a bigger magnet.'

Revathi was not sure. She had seen something, and it had been too quick to catch. She put the engine and the carriage back on the table, and set them going again. This time she watched the engine, and not the carriage.
There it was. Just as the carriage shot forward, the engine twitched. It rolled a tiny way backwards, towards the carriage, and then they met.
'Did you see?' she said. 'The engine moved! It has the magnet, and it moved. So the carriage is pulling it too.'
'Nonsense,' said Uncle Mohan. 'A nail cannot pull. It has no power in it.'

Her little sister Sowmya, who was six, had been sitting under the table with a lump of clay. She popped her head up. 'Uncle, what if you put the nail in the front and the magnet in the back and held the nail with your hand?'

Nobody answered her, so she took the carriage in one hand and the magnet engine in the other, and set them far apart on the table. She let go of both at once. The engine slid towards the carriage. The carriage slid towards the engine. They met in the middle of the table, exactly half way.
Revathi's uncle stopped talking. Ajji, who had been turning a top on the lathe, switched it off and came to look. 'Do it again,' she said.

Sowmya did it again. And again. Then she put a big lump of clay in the carriage, so it was much heavier. This time the engine slid nearly all the way across the table, and the heavy carriage only crept a little way to meet it.

'It is the same pull,' said Revathi slowly. 'The nail pulls the magnet as hard as the magnet pulls the nail. But the light one moves further. That is why the engine only twitched in my first try. It was much heavier than the carriage, so the carriage did the running.'
'And that is why the carriage banged into the engine and chipped the red lacquer,' said Ajji. 'A light thing coming fast. If a bigger magnet pulled harder, the bang would be even worse.'

So they did the opposite of what Uncle Mohan said. They used a smaller magnet, so the pull was gentle. They made the engine and the carriages weigh the same, by adding a pinch of clay to the lighter ones. Now whenever Revathi set them on the table, the engine and the carriage slid towards each other and met softly in the middle with a little click, like two people shaking hands.

Mrs Khan ordered two hundred trains. Uncle Mohan painted the faces on every one, and he was quiet for a whole week. At the end of the week, he put a small magnet into his pocket. 'For Sowmya,' he said. 'For asking the question that nobody asked.'
story.epiphany: A magnet and a nail pull each other with exactly equal force. The engine twitched backwards because the carriage was pulling it. The lighter carriage moved further because the same pull moves a light thing faster than a heavy thing. A gentle meeting needs a smaller pull and balanced weights.
ask: Why did the engine twitch backwards when the carriage rushed forward?
When Sowmya let go of the engine and the carriage together, where did they meet? Why there?
Why did the carriage move further when it was light and the engine heavy?
Uncle Mohan was sure the nail could not pull. What would you have said to him, using only what you can see?
A six-year-old asked the question that nobody asked. Why do you think questions from the youngest are sometimes the best?

games.title: Who Moves More? The pull-in-pairs card game
games.context: This is a guessing game about pulls that come in pairs. Each card shows two things pulling or pushing each other. You say which one moves more, or if neither moves, and then check the back.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile and four kinds of tokens laid out in a row on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the others hold a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the card. Everyone puts a token face down.

setup.art: Players turning their tokens over together and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: two things pulling or pushing on the front, who moves more on the back

items.f: FIRST: a magnet on a light raft. SECOND: a steel nail on a raft with the same mass. The rafts float 8 cm apart. Who moves more?
items.b: Both the same. The two pulls are equal and the masses are equal, so the rafts meet in the middle.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet on a light raft. SECOND: a nail on a raft three times as heavy. Who moves more?
items.b: First moves more. The pulls are equal, but the heavier raft is harder to get moving.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet on a raft. SECOND: a wooden pencil on a raft of the same mass. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves. Wood is not a magnetic material, so there is no magnetic pull to move either raft.

items.f: FIRST: a small fridge magnet. SECOND: a heavy iron almirah on a rough floor. Both are let go near each other. Who moves more?
items.b: First moves more. The almirah is pulled just as hard, but its mass and the friction on the floor keep it still.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet held still in a clamp. SECOND: a steel nail on a floating raft. Who moves more?
items.b: Second moves more. The clamp holds the magnet still, so only the free nail moves. The nail still pulls the magnet with an equal force.

items.f: FIRST: a strong neodymium magnet on a raft. SECOND: a weak fridge magnet on a raft of the same mass. Who moves more?
items.b: Both the same. There is only one pair of forces between them, so the strong magnet cannot pull harder than it is pulled.

items.f: FIRST: a brass key on a raft. SECOND: an aluminium foil ball on a raft. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves. Brass and aluminium are not magnetic, and neither is a magnet.

items.f: FIRST: a plain iron nail on a raft. SECOND: another plain iron nail on a raft. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves. Neither nail is a magnet, so they have nothing to pull each other with.

items.f: FIRST: a magnetised needle on a raft. SECOND: a magnet on a raft of the same mass. They face each other with opposite poles. Who moves more?
items.b: Both the same. Opposite poles attract, with equal pulls, and equal masses move equally.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet on a raft. SECOND: a magnet on a raft of the same mass, with the same poles facing. Who moves more?
items.b: Both the same. The two push each other apart equally. A push is also a pair of equal forces.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet in your hand. SECOND: a steel pin on a thread, hanging beside it. Who moves more?
items.b: Second moves more. The magnet pulls your hand too, but your hand has far too much mass to move.

items.f: FIRST: a girl of 30 kilograms on roller skates. SECOND: a woman of 60 kilograms on roller skates. They hold a rope and the girl pulls. Who moves more?
items.b: First moves more. The rope pulls both equally, so the lighter skater moves twice as far.

items.f: FIRST: two girls of the same weight on roller skates, holding a rope. One of them pulls. Who moves more?
items.b: Both the same. Both feel the same pull from the rope, so both slide towards each other.

items.f: FIRST: a girl on roller skates pushing a wall. SECOND: the wall. Who moves more?
items.b: First moves more. The wall pushes back equally, and the girl rolls away. The wall is part of a building, and it does not move.

items.f: FIRST: the Earth. SECOND: an apple falling from a tree. Who moves more?
items.b: Second moves more. The apple pulls the Earth with the same force, but the Earth has so much mass that it moves by a tiny amount nobody can see.

items.f: FIRST: a plastic comb, rubbed on dry hair. SECOND: a small scrap of paper. Who moves more?
items.b: Second moves more. The pull is static electricity and is equal both ways, but the paper is much lighter.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet in the left hand. SECOND: a nail in the right hand. Both are held tight. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves, but each hand feels the pull. Equal pulls are felt whether or not anything moves.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet on a raft. SECOND: a nail on a raft 1 metre away. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves. A magnet's pull gets much weaker with distance, and at 1 metre it is too small to move a raft.

items.f: FIRST: a bar magnet on a raft. SECOND: a stroked needle on a raft of the same mass. The north end of the needle faces the north pole of the bar. Who moves more?
items.b: Both the same. The two push each other apart with equal forces, which also proves that the needle is a real magnet.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet taped to a heavy brick. SECOND: a nail on a light raft. Who moves more?
items.b: Second moves more. The pulls are equal, but the brick is far heavier than the raft.

items.f: FIRST: a plain steel nail held in your hand. SECOND: a small paper clip hanging from a thread beside it. No magnet is near. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves. A plain nail is not a magnet, so it has almost no pull on the clip.

items.f: FIRST: a large iron nail on a light raft. SECOND: three small paper clips on a raft of the same mass. A magnet is held still between them. Who moves more?
items.b: The magnet pulls each one with a different force. The one with more iron close to the magnet usually moves faster. Test it and see.

items.f: FIRST: a magnet on a raft. SECOND: a copper coin on a raft of the same mass. Who moves more?
items.b: Neither moves. Copper is not a magnetic material, so there is nothing to pull the coin.

items.f: FIRST: a hanging magnet on a long thread. SECOND: a steel nail held in your fingers. The magnet swings. Who moves more?
items.b: First moves more. The magnet is free to swing, and the nail is held. The nail is still pulling the magnet.

printables.title: 16 tokens: four each of First moves more, Second moves more, Both the same, and Neither moves

rules: You need the cards, the 16 tokens and a pencil and paper for scores. Each player takes one token of each kind.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front out loud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. They should be ready to say why. If you are playing alone, say your answer out loud and turn the card over.
Everyone turns their token over together. The reader turns the card and reads the back out loud.
A player with the right token wins 1 point. A player with the right token and a good reason wins 2 points.
A good reason mentions the pull being equal, the mass of the thing, or the material being magnetic or not.

After each card, the next player becomes the reader. Play 12 cards, and try to give everyone the same number of turns as reader. The player with the most points wins. If you are playing alone, count how many of the 12 you got right.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 16 tokens. Shuffle the cards. Give every player four tokens, one of each kind.
flow.say: Each card shows two things pulling or pushing each other. You guess which one moves more, or if nothing moves. Then we check the back.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take one token of each kind.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Moves More. You get the cards and tokens ready.

flow.do: Play the first four cards. After each one, read the back aloud and ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone puts a token face down and turns it over together. Who got a point? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: On a card with a magnet and a nail, which one pulls harder?
good: They pull equally.
The magnet pulls the nail and the nail pulls the magnet just as hard.
Neither one pulls harder. Each pulls the other equally.

flow.parent: Many children say the magnet pulls harder. Do not correct them yet. Let the backs of the cards show them, and watch whether the answer changes by the fourth card.
flow.context: In this step you play the first four cards and score your points.

flow.do: Play four more cards. These cards have people on roller skates, or the Earth and an apple. Ask the question below after the last one.
flow.say: These cards have people and planets, but the rule is the same. Does the rule about equal pulls still work?
flow.kid: Play four more cards. People and planets follow the same rule.

ask.q: Does the rule about equal pulls work for people on skates as well as for magnets?
good: Yes, the rope pulls both skaters equally.
Yes, a pull always comes in a pair.
Yes, the lighter skater moves further.

flow.parent: If your child is surprised that the Earth moves when an apple falls, say that it moves by an amount far too small to see. The rule still holds.
flow.context: In this step you play cards with skaters and the Earth, to see that the same rule works everywhere.

flow.do: Play four more cards. When a card says that two rafts have the same mass, ask what would change if one raft were heavier.
flow.say: Keep going. When both things have the same mass, think what happens if one of them gets heavier. Which one would move less?
flow.kid: Play four more cards. Think about what happens when one thing is heavier.

check.q: A magnet and a nail pull each other. Which sentence is true?
options: The magnet pulls harder because it is the magnet
The two pulls are exactly equal
The nail pulls harder because it is heavier
check.why: The two pulls are always equal and opposite. Picking 'the magnet pulls harder' is the most common guess. It comes from watching the nail move and forgetting that the magnet is held in a hand.

flow.context: In this step you play more cards and check your idea about equal pulls.

flow.do: Add up the points and name the winner. Then talk about the card that surprised each player most.
flow.say: Who won? Which card surprised you most? What did you think before, and what do you think now?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card surprised you most?
flow.think: Can you think of two things that pull or push each other, where only one of them moves?
flow.context: In this last step you add up the points and talk about what surprised you.

games.title: Keep or Drop? The soft and hard magnet game
games.context: This is a sorting game about soft and hard magnetic materials. Each card names a job. You decide if the magnet in it must keep its magnetism, which needs a hard material, or let go of it, which needs a soft one.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a pile and two sorting mats marked KEEP and DROP on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the two mats. Put the mats side by side.

setup.art: A child placing a card for a loudspeaker magnet on the KEEP mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it on KEEP or DROP and give a reason.

setup.art: A parent turning a card over to show the answer and reason on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check your answer.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a job on the front, KEEP (hard material) or DROP (soft material) with the reason on the back

items.f: The magnet in a loudspeaker.
items.b: KEEP. It must stay a magnet for years, so it is made of a hard magnetic material.

items.f: The iron core inside an electric bell.
items.b: DROP. The core must stop being a magnet when the electricity stops, so it is made of a soft magnetic material.

items.f: A compass needle.
items.b: KEEP. The needle must stay a magnet to turn to north, so it is hard steel.

items.f: The lifting magnet on a scrapyard crane that drops its load.
items.b: DROP. The core is soft iron, so the load falls when the electricity is switched off.

items.f: A fridge magnet.
items.b: KEEP. It is a permanent magnet made of ferrite, a hard magnetic material.

items.f: The core of a transformer.
items.b: DROP. It must follow the changing electric current, so it is made of thin sheets of soft iron.

items.f: The coating on a hard disk.
items.b: KEEP. The tiny regions must stay turned for years, so the coating is a hard magnetic material.

items.f: The dark stripe on an old bank card.
items.b: KEEP. The stripe holds information as long as the card lasts, so it is a hard magnetic material.

items.f: An ordinary iron nail.
items.b: DROP. A plain nail is a soft magnetic material and loses most of its magnetism when the magnet goes.

items.f: A sewing needle.
items.b: KEEP. A needle is made of hard steel and keeps its magnetism for days or weeks.

items.f: A magnetic door catch on a cupboard.
items.b: KEEP. The magnet must go on pulling the door shut every day, so it is a hard magnetic material.

items.f: The cores of the coils inside an electric fan motor.
items.b: DROP. The cores follow the changing current, so they are made of soft iron sheets.

items.f: A magnet in earphones.
items.b: KEEP. A small strong magnet works with a coil to make sound, so it is a hard magnetic material.

items.f: A relay, a small switch that clicks when electricity flows.
items.b: DROP. The relay has a soft iron core that becomes a magnet only when the current flows.

items.f: A cassette tape.
items.b: KEEP. The tape is coated with a hard magnetic powder so the recorded sound lasts.

items.f: A paper clip that is magnetised by touching a magnet.
items.b: DROP. A paper clip is a fairly soft magnetic material and loses most of its magnetism.

items.f: A horseshoe magnet in a school lab.
items.b: KEEP. It is a permanent magnet made of a hard material such as steel or alnico.

items.f: The bolt used as a core for a homemade electromagnet.
items.b: DROP. Use soft iron, so that the bolt stops being a magnet when the battery is disconnected.

items.f: A magnetic strip on a fridge door seal.
items.b: KEEP. The strip must stay magnetised for years to keep pulling the door shut.

items.f: The needle of a school ammeter that is moved by a coil.
items.b: KEEP. A small permanent magnet is used so that the needle moves in the same direction every time.

printables.title: 2 sorting mats: KEEP (hard magnetic material) and DROP (soft magnetic material)
items: KEEP: the magnet must stay magnetic for years. Hard magnetic material.
DROP: the magnet must switch off when the job is done. Soft magnetic material.

rules: You need the 20 cards and the two mats. Lay the mats side by side. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read the front out loud. Do not turn it over yet.
Put the card on KEEP or DROP and give one reason. Other players say if they agree.
Turn the card over and read the back out loud. If you were right, you keep the card. If you were wrong, put the card back at the bottom of the pile.
A right answer with a good reason wins two cards, and a right answer with no reason wins one card. A good reason says how long the magnet must last.
Play until the pile is finished. The player with the most cards wins. Playing alone, count how many cards you got right out of 20.
If two players disagree about a card, test the idea by asking: does this magnet need to last for years, or switch off when the job is done? The back of the card decides.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the two mats. Lay the mats side by side and shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Some magnets must keep their magnetism for years. Some must let go the moment the job is done. Keep or drop? That is your guess for each card.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mats. Put the mats side by side. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Keep or Drop. You get the cards and mats ready.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each one, turn the card over and read the reason.
flow.say: Read the job. Does the magnet in it need to stay magnetic for years, or does it need to switch off? Put it on the mat and say why.
flow.kid: Read a card. Keep or drop? Put it on a mat. Say why. Check the back.

ask.q: What is the difference between the cards on KEEP and the cards on DROP?
good: KEEP jobs need a magnet that lasts.
DROP jobs need a magnet that can switch off.
KEEP jobs use hard materials and DROP jobs use soft materials.

flow.parent: The word 'soft' is easy to mix up with squashy. Remind your child that here it only means that the material loses its magnetism easily.
flow.context: In this step you play the first six cards and look for the pattern.

flow.do: Play the next six cards. Before each one, say whether you think the job needs a hard material or a soft one. Ask the question below after the last one.
flow.say: Look for the pattern now. What do all the KEEP jobs have in common? What do the DROP jobs have in common?
flow.kid: Play six more cards. Look for a pattern in the KEEP cards and the DROP cards.

ask.q: What do you notice about the jobs on the DROP mat?
good: They all have electricity or a coil.
The magnet has to switch off.
They need to let go of something.

flow.context: In this step you play six more cards and look for the pattern.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards. Stop at a card with a coil of wire and ask the check question.
flow.say: Some of these jobs use a coil of wire and electricity. A coil can make a magnet that switches on and off. What must the middle of the coil be made of?
flow.kid: Play the last eight cards. Some use a coil. Think about what the middle of the coil must be made of.

check.q: An electric crane uses a magnet to lift scrap iron, and must drop the scrap when the electricity is off. What should the core be made of?
options: Hard steel, so it keeps its magnetism
Soft iron, so it loses its magnetism when the electricity stops
Wood, because it is light
check.why: Soft iron becomes a strong magnet when the current flows and loses it as soon as the current stops, so the load drops. Hard steel would keep part of its magnetism and the scrap would stay stuck.

flow.context: In this step you play the last eight cards and meet the coil and the switch.

flow.do: Count the cards each player won. Name the winner. Then ask each player which card changed their mind.
flow.say: Who won? Which card changed your mind about hard and soft?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which card changed your mind?
flow.think: A material that is good for one job can be bad for another. Can you think of another case where that is true?
flow.context: In this last step you count the cards and talk about what changed your mind.

experiments.title: Rafts on the Water: does the nail pull the magnet too?
experiments.question: A magnet picks up a nail. If we put the magnet and the nail on floating rafts, will only the nail move, only the magnet, or both? And does it change if one raft is heavier?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When a magnet on a raft and a nail on a raft are 8 centimetres apart, which raft will move, or will both? What if the nail raft is three times as heavy? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every trial uses the same tub, the same still water and the same starting gap of 8 centimetres. The two rafts are made the same size and, except in the last trial, the same mass. We wait for the water to go still before each trial and let go of both rafts at the same moment. Only one thing changes at a time: first a wooden pencil in place of the nails, as a control, then the nail raft held still, then both rafts free, then a heavy nail raft. Each trial is done three times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Where they met (cm from the magnet's start)

materials.item: a wide plastic tub or basin at least 35 cm long, with 4 cm of water, not a steel vessel
2 rafts, each about 6 cm square, cut from thermocol packaging or from thin foam, or 2 plastic bottle lids
a strong magnet, a ceramic disc, a small bar or a neodymium magnet
3 steel nails, about 4 cm long
a wooden pencil stub, as a control
modelling clay or a ball of atta dough, to balance the rafts
a 30 cm ruler, laid across the top of the tub
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Keep magnets away from phones, watches and bank cards. Keep the magnet and nails away from children under five, who might put them in their mouths. Wipe up spills so nobody slips.
experiments.record: For every trial write how far each raft moved, in centimetres. Do each trial three times and write down the middle value. Then draw a bar for the magnet raft and a bar for the nail raft in each trial.

schedule.what: Build the rafts, run the control, then three trials with three tries each. Write what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you float a magnet on one raft and a nail on another, and find out which one moves. It tests whether the nail pulls the magnet too.

setup.art: A plastic tub with 4 centimetres of water, a ruler laid across the top and two small rafts floating 8 centimetres apart.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the tub. Lay the ruler across it. Float the rafts 8 cm apart.

setup.art: Two rafts, one carrying a round magnet and one carrying three nails, with a small ball of clay on the lighter one.
setup.caption: 2. Put the magnet on one raft and the nails on the other. Add clay until both sit equally low.

setup.art: The two rafts sailing towards each other and touching in the middle of the tub, with the ruler marks visible.
setup.caption: 3. Let go of both rafts at once. Read how far each one moved.

setup.art: A raft with a large lump of clay and the nails next to a raft with the magnet, with the magnet raft nearly at the heavy raft.
setup.caption: 4. Make the nail raft heavy with clay. Try again.

setup.art: A bar chart on paper with a tall bar for the magnet raft and a short bar for the heavy nail raft.
setup.caption: 5. Draw a bar for each raft in each trial.

flow.do: Show your child the tub, the rafts, the magnet and the nails. Ask for a guess and a reason for each question. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will float a magnet on one raft and a nail on another, 8 centimetres apart. What do you think will happen? Will only one raft move, or both? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A magnet on one raft. A nail on another. What will happen? Why do you think so?

ask.q: What do you think the nail raft will do when the magnet raft comes close?
good: It will stay still, because a nail cannot pull.
It will move too, because the magnet pulls it.
It will move a little.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Most children say only the nail moves, and a few say the magnet. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the exact words down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rafts experiment. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut two rafts of the same size. Put the magnet on one raft and three nails on the other. Float both in the middle of the tub. Add a pinch of clay to the lighter one until both rafts float equally low.
flow.say: We need two rafts with the same mass. If one raft were heavier, it would be harder to move. So add clay to the lighter one until both rafts sit at the same height in the water.
flow.kid: Put the magnet on one raft. Put three nails on the other. Add clay until both sit equally low.
flow.parent: A kitchen scale makes this easier. If you have one, weigh both rafts and add clay to make them equal. If the rafts tip, stick the magnet down with a little clay. Keep the tub away from any steel sink, almirah or gas stove, because steel nearby can pull a raft.
flow.context: In this step you build the two rafts and make their masses equal.

flow.do: Swap the nails for a wooden pencil stub on the nail raft. Wait for the water to go still. Put the rafts 8 cm apart and let go of both. Watch for 20 seconds. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: First we run a control. We put a pencil on one raft instead of the nails. If the rafts move now, something other than magnetism is moving them. Does anything happen?
flow.kid: Put a pencil on one raft. No nails. Let go of both rafts. Does anything happen?

check.q: Why do we run a trial with a wooden pencil in place of the nails first?
options: To see if the rafts move by themselves, from ripples or the water
Because wood is the best raft
To make the magnet stronger
check.why: A control trial swaps out the one thing we want to test, here the nails. If the rafts do not move with a pencil, then the moves in the next trials must come from the nails. Picking 'wood is the best raft' mixes up the raft with the thing on it.

flow.parent: Nothing should happen. If the rafts drift together, they are too close. Floating things within about 2 centimetres pull each other together because of the water's skin. That is why we start 8 centimetres apart. If they drift, wait longer for the water to calm and try again.
flow.context: In this step you run a control trial, with a pencil instead of the nails.

flow.do: Put the nails back on the nail raft. Hold the nail raft still with the tip of a pencil against its far edge. Let go of the magnet raft only. Read how far the magnet raft moves. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now the nail raft is held still with a pencil. We let the magnet raft go. Which way does it go? And how far?
flow.kid: Hold the nail raft still. Let the magnet raft go. Which way does it go?

ask.q: The nail raft is held still. Why did the magnet raft move to it?
good: The nail pulled the magnet.
The pull works both ways.
The nail was pulling the magnet, and the magnet was free to move.

flow.parent: A ceramic magnet may need to start closer, perhaps 5 centimetres, to move a raft. If nothing moves at 8 centimetres, move both rafts closer by 1 centimetre at a time. Use the same starting gap for all your trials.
flow.context: In this step the nail raft is held still and only the magnet raft is free. You see if the magnet moves.

flow.do: Take the pencil away. Float both rafts 8 cm apart, wait for the water to go still, and let go of both together. When they touch, read how far each one moved. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now both rafts are free. Let go of both at the same time. Where do they meet? Does one move more than the other?
flow.kid: Let go of both rafts together. Where do they meet? Did both move?

check.q: Both rafts have the same mass, and they meet in the middle. What does this show?
options: The magnet pulls the nail, and the nail does not pull the magnet
The magnet and the nail pull each other with equal force
The nail is stronger than the magnet
check.why: If the pulls were different, the raft pulled harder would stay nearer to where it began. They meet in the middle, so the pulls are equal. Picking 'the nail does not pull' goes against what you saw, because the nail raft moved.

flow.parent: Typically the rafts meet near the middle, with each moving a similar distance. Small differences come from the clay, ripples and the raft shape. Write exactly what you see.
flow.context: In this step both rafts are free. You see where they meet.

flow.do: Add two big balls of clay to the nail raft, so it is about three times as heavy as the magnet raft. Float both 8 cm apart and let go together. Read how far each one moves. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now the nail raft is heavy. Same magnet, same nails, same gap. What happens this time? Which raft moves more?
flow.kid: Add lots of clay to the nail raft. Let go of both together. Which raft moves more?

ask.q: Did the heavy nail raft feel a smaller pull than the magnet raft?
good: No, the pull was the same, but it is harder to move a heavy raft.
The pull was equal and the heavy one moved less.
The pull on both rafts was the same, and the heavy one needs more push to move.

flow.parent: The magnet raft should now travel most of the way, and the heavy raft only creeps. If the heavy raft does not move at all, that is fine. The magnet raft still moved because of the nail's pull on it.
flow.context: In this step the nail raft is made heavy. You see how the mass changes who moves.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then draw the bar chart.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the magnet and the nail pull each other equally. What I saw: when both rafts were free they met in the middle, and when the nail raft was heavy it moved less. Why: the pulls are a pair of equal forces, and the force moves light things further than heavy things.
flow.context: In this last step you say what you think, what you saw and why, and draw your results.

experiments.title: The Hanging V: why do two nails spread apart?
experiments.question: If two nails hang side by side from one magnet, will they hang straight, stick together, or spread apart? And do longer nails spread further?
experiments.predict: Before you start, draw what you think two hanging nails will look like. Then guess. Will the two free ends hang straight down, move together or spread apart? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same magnet and hold it still above the table. We touch the heads of the nails to the same flat face of the magnet, side by side. We measure the gap between the tips with the same ruler held in the same place. Only the nail length changes, so any difference in the gap comes from the length. Each pair is tested three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a strong magnet with a flat face, a ceramic disc or a neodymium magnet
4 steel nails with heads: 2 short ones about 3 cm long and 2 long ones about 6 cm long
a 30 cm ruler
a sheet of paper behind, and a pencil
a small bowl, to put the nails in afterwards

experiments.safety: Nails have sharp points. Hold them by the head and keep the points away from faces. A grown-up should stay beside a younger child. Keep magnets away from phones and bank cards.
experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the magnet and the two nails in each try, and draw the V of the hanging tips to scale.

schedule.what: Hang two short nails and two long nails from the magnet. Measure the tip gap three times each. Add a third nail. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you hang nails from a magnet and find out why they do not hang straight down. You measure the gap between their tips.

setup.art: A round magnet held above a table with two short nails hanging from its flat face by their heads.
setup.caption: 1. Touch the heads of two short nails to the flat face of the magnet.

setup.art: A ruler laid flat on the table under the nail tips, showing the gap between them.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the ruler under the tips and read the gap.

setup.art: The same magnet with two long nails hanging in a wider V.
setup.caption: 3. Try two long nails. Read the gap again.

setup.art: A magnet with three nails hanging in a small bunch with their tips pushing apart.
setup.caption: 4. Hang a third nail. Look at the three tips.

flow.do: Show your child the magnet and the nails. Ask them to draw what two hanging nails will look like, then to guess and give a reason.
flow.say: I will hang two nails from the magnet, side by side. Draw what you think they will look like. Will they hang straight, or lean in, or lean out? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two nails hang from a magnet. Draw them. Will they hang straight? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the nails will hang that way?
good: They are both heavy, so they hang straight down.
They are both pulled to the magnet, so they will lean together.
They push each other apart.

flow.parent: Do not correct the drawing. Most children draw two parallel nails hanging straight down. Keep the drawing to compare with the result.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hanging V test. You draw and guess before you try.

flow.do: Hold the magnet still above the table. Touch the heads of the two short nails to its flat face, side by side. Let go gently. Look at the tips.
flow.say: Touch the heads of two nails to the flat face of the magnet, side by side. Let go gently. What do the tips do? Do they hang straight?
flow.kid: Touch two nail heads to the magnet. Let go gently. What do the tips do?
flow.parent: The tips should hang apart in a V, though the gap may be small, around half a centimetre to two centimetres. If the nails will not hang, use a stronger magnet or lighter, thinner nails. If the V is too small to see, hold a sheet of paper behind and look from the side.

check.q: The two nail tips spread apart. What is the best explanation?
options: Both tips became the same kind of pole, so they repel
The nails are too heavy to hang straight
The tips are attracted to the table
check.why: Each nail becomes an induced magnet. The heads touch the same pole of the magnet, so both heads get the same pole, and both tips get the opposite one. Two poles of the same kind repel. If the nails were just too heavy, they would hang straight down.

flow.context: In this step you hang the first two nails and see the V.

flow.do: Lay the ruler flat on the table under the tips, close to them. Read the gap between the two tips. Do it 3 times, each time hanging the nails again. Write the middle value.
flow.say: Measure the gap between the tips. Hang the nails again and measure again, three times in all. The middle number is the one we use.
flow.kid: Measure the gap between the tips. Do it 3 times. Pick the middle number.

ask.q: Why do we hang the nails again and measure three times?
good: One try can be a fluke.
The gap changes a little each time.
Every nail hangs a little differently each time.

flow.context: In this step you measure the tip gap for the short nails, three times.

flow.do: Do the same with the two long nails. Read the gap three times. Write the middle value.
flow.say: Now try the two long nails. Is the V wider or narrower? Why do you think that is?
flow.kid: Hang the two long nails. Measure the gap 3 times. Is the V wider?
flow.parent: Usually the long nails have a wider gap at the tips, because the tips are further from the magnet and freer to move apart. If your result is the other way round, write it honestly. A weak magnet may hold a long nail with a different tilt, and that is worth noting.
flow.context: In this step you test the long nails and compare the two V shapes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened. Then add a third nail and look at the tips.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened? Then hang a third nail. What do the three tips do?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened. Then add a third nail.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the nails become magnets and their tips repel. What I saw: the tips spread into a V, wider for the long nails. Why: each nail became a magnet with the same pole at its tip, and two of the same pole repel.
flow.context: In this last step you say what you think, what you saw and why, then try three nails.

experiments.title: Soft or Hard? Which steel keeps its magnetism?
experiments.question: If we stroke a nail, a needle, a pin and a paper clip with the same magnet, which one keeps its magnetism the longest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, line up the four things from the one you think will keep its magnetism longest to the one that will lose it first. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We stroke each thing the same number of times, 40, with the same magnet, in the same direction. We test each one with the same heap of staples, the same way, at the same times. Only the thing changes, so any difference comes from the steel. Each test is done three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a strong magnet, a ceramic bar or a neodymium magnet
1 steel nail, about 6 cm, 1 sewing needle, 1 steel pin and 1 paper clip
about 30 small office staples in a heap on a plate
a clock or a phone timer, kept away from the magnet
a table to tap them on, and a pencil with the results table
a small plate to hold the heap of staples

experiments.safety: A needle and a pin are sharp. A grown-up handles them and puts them away afterwards. Staples are small and sharp, so keep them away from children under five. Keep the magnet away from phones and cards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table for every thing. Then draw a bar for each thing, as tall as the number of staples it held right after, and another bar, in a different colour, as tall as the number it held the next day.

schedule.what: Stroke each thing 40 times. Count the staples it lifts right after, after 10 minutes, and after 20 taps.
Count the staples each thing lifts the next day. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you magnetise four steel things and find out which one keeps its magnetism. It tests the difference between soft and hard magnetic materials.

setup.art: A hand stroking a steel nail from head to tip along the end of a magnet, lifting it high to come back.
setup.caption: 1. Stroke each thing 40 times with the magnet, always the same way.

setup.art: The tip of a needle dipped into a heap of small staples with a few staples clinging to it.
setup.caption: 2. Dip the end in the heap of staples. Count the staples that cling.

setup.art: A nail being tapped on a table and then dipped in the heap of staples again.
setup.caption: 3. Tap it 20 times on the table. Count again.

setup.art: A table with rows for a nail, a needle, a pin and a clip and columns for the counts of staples.
setup.caption: 4. Write all the counts in the table and test again the next day.

flow.do: Line up the nail, needle, pin and paper clip. Ask your child to put them in order from keeps the magnetism longest to loses it first, and to give a reason. Write the order down.
flow.say: We will make each of these a magnet with the same magnet, in the same way. Which one will keep its magnetism longest? Which will lose it first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Line them up. Which keeps the magnetism longest? Which loses it first? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will keep its magnetism longest?
good: It is the thickest.
It is the hardest.
It is made of the best metal.

flow.parent: Do not correct the order. Children often say the biggest, thickest thing will keep it longest. Write the order to compare later.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Soft or Hard test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Test each thing on the heap of staples first, before any stroking. Then stroke the nail 40 times with one end of the magnet, from the nail's head to its tip. After each stroke, lift the magnet high to come back to the head. Do not stroke back and forth.
flow.say: First test every thing on the staples before stroking, to see if it was already a magnet. Then stroke the nail from head to tip, 40 times, always the same way. Lift the magnet high to come back to the head.
flow.kid: Test it on the staples first. Then stroke it 40 times, always one way.
flow.parent: Stroke each thing in the same direction and use the same end of the same magnet. Count in tens. The needle and pin are sharp, so a grown-up strokes them, holding the eye end down on a table with a finger. Do the nail first.
flow.context: In this step you check each thing before stroking, and you stroke the nail.

flow.do: Right after stroking the nail, dip its tip into the heap of staples and lift. Count how many cling. Write the number. Stroke and test the needle, the pin and the paper clip in the same way.
