flow.say: Dip the end into the staples and lift. Count how many cling. Do the same for every thing, as soon as you have stroked it.
flow.kid: Dip the tip in the staples. Lift. Count how many cling. Do this for each one.
flow.parent: Test the same end each time, the end that touched the magnet last. A nail might lift 5 to 10 staples. A needle might lift fewer at first, because it is thinner. Write whatever you see.
flow.context: In this step you count the staples each thing holds right after stroking.

flow.do: Wait 10 minutes. Count the staples each thing lifts again. Then tap each one on the table 20 times and count again. Write all the numbers.
flow.say: Wait ten minutes. Test again. Then tap each one on the table twenty times, and test again. What changes?
flow.kid: Wait 10 minutes. Test again. Tap each one 20 times. Test again.

check.q: After 10 minutes the nail lifts fewer staples than before, and the needle lifts almost the same. What does this show?
options: The needle is a harder magnetic material than the nail
The needle is made of a different metal that is not steel
The nail was never magnetised
check.why: The domains in the needle stay turned, and those in the nail turn back. This is the difference between a hard and a soft magnetic material. Picking 'never magnetised' is wrong because the nail did lift staples right after the stroking.

flow.context: In this step you wait, tap, and test again.

flow.do: The next day, test every thing again on the staples, and write the numbers. Then draw the bar chart.
flow.say: A day has passed. Test each thing on the staples again. Which ones still have some magnetism?
flow.kid: A day later, test each one on the staples. Which ones still hold some?
flow.parent: The needle and pin may still hold a few staples. The nail may hold none or one. Your numbers may differ, because the steel in nails, needles and clips differs from maker to maker. Write what you see.
flow.context: In this step you test the next day to see which thing still has magnetism.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: harder steel keeps its magnetism longer than soft iron. What I saw: the needle still held staples the next day, and the nail held none. Why: in hard steel the domains are held in place, and in soft iron they turn back.
flow.context: In this last step you say what you think, what you saw and why.

activities.title: Hold Still, Magnet! A hanging magnet and a nail

materials.item: a magnet that is small and light, a ceramic disc or a neodymium magnet
a steel nail
40 cm of thread, tied round the magnet or taped to it
a pencil, and tape to hold it across the table edge

schedule.what: Hang the magnet. Bring a nail near it. Then hang the nail and bring the magnet near it.

activities.record: Draw the hanging magnet before and after the nail comes near it, and write one sentence about what you saw.
activities.context: In this short activity, you hang a magnet on a thread and bring a nail close. You see which one moves.

setup.art: A pencil taped across the edge of a table with a thread hanging from it and a small magnet tied at the end.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a pencil over the table edge. Hang the magnet from a thread.

setup.art: A hand holding a steel nail near the hanging magnet, which leans towards the nail.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the nail 3 cm from the magnet, without touching. Watch.

setup.art: A child drawing the magnet leaning towards the nail in a notebook.
setup.caption: 3. Swap them. Hang the nail and hold the magnet. Draw what you see.

flow.do: Tape the pencil across the table edge, so it sticks out. Tie the thread to the pencil and hang the magnet from it. Wait until it hangs still. Ask your child to guess what the magnet will do when a nail comes near.
flow.say: Here is a magnet hanging from a thread. I will hold a nail near it, but not touch it. What will the magnet do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A magnet hangs on a thread. What will it do when a nail comes near? Why?

ask.q: Will the magnet move, or will it stay still?
good: It will stay still, because the nail is not a magnet.
It will lean towards the nail.
It will move a little.

flow.parent: Keep the table away from any steel. Do not correct the guess. Most children say the magnet will stay still.
flow.context: This is the first step of Hold Still, Magnet. You guess before you try.

flow.do: Hold the nail about 3 cm from the magnet, level with it, and not touching. Hold it still and watch. Move it a little closer if nothing happens.
flow.say: Hold the nail still, a few centimetres away. Watch the magnet. What does it do?
flow.kid: Hold the nail still, a little way from the magnet. Watch the magnet.

check.q: The hanging magnet leans towards the held nail. What does this show?
options: The nail pulls the magnet
The thread is pulling the magnet
The magnet is pulling itself
check.why: The magnet was free to move, and it moved to the nail. So the nail was pulling the magnet. Picking 'the thread' is a natural guess, but the thread only holds the magnet up and cannot pull it sideways.

flow.context: In this step you hold the nail near the hanging magnet and see what the magnet does.

flow.do: Now hang the nail from the thread instead, and hold the magnet near it. Watch the nail. Then say what you think the nail and the magnet do to each other.
flow.say: Now we swap. The nail hangs and I hold the magnet. What does the nail do? What does that tell us about the pull?
flow.kid: Hang the nail. Hold the magnet near it. Which one moves now?
flow.think: When the magnet hung from the thread, the magnet moved. When the nail hung from the thread, the nail moved. Who was doing the pulling each time?
flow.parent: The nail swings towards the magnet, and the hanging magnet swung towards the nail. Both are pulled. Whichever one is free to move is the one you see move.
flow.context: In this step you swap the nail and the magnet, and see that the free one always moves.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things: what you think, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the nail pulls the magnet too. What I saw: the hanging magnet leaned to the held nail. Why: the pull works both ways, and the thing that is free to move is the thing that moves.
flow.context: In this last step you say what you think, what you saw and why.

activities.title: Magnet or Just Iron? The repel test

materials.item: a magnet to be your tester, hung on a thread or floating on a raft in water
5 mystery pieces: a stroked needle, a plain nail, a second magnet, a steel bolt and a steel spoon, each with a letter on a paper tag
a grown-up helper to prepare the mystery pieces in secret
a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: The helper prepares five mystery pieces. Test both ends of each. Sort them into magnets and plain iron. Then the helper says which were magnets.

activities.record: A table with five rows, A to E. For each, write what end 1 did and what end 2 did, and your verdict: magnet or plain iron.
activities.context: In this activity, you use a magnet as a tester to find out which of five mystery pieces are real magnets and which are only magnetic.

setup.art: Five mystery pieces labelled A to E in a row on a table, beside a magnet hanging from a thread.
setup.caption: 1. A helper labels the five pieces A to E and hides which are magnets.

setup.art: A hand bringing one end of a piece near the hanging magnet, which swings away.
setup.caption: 2. Bring one end near the hanging magnet. Does it pull or push?

setup.art: The same piece turned round and its other end brought near, with the magnet swinging towards it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the piece round. Test the other end.

flow.do: A grown-up helper strokes one needle 40 times with a magnet, to make it a magnet. The helper then gathers five pieces: the stroked needle, a plain nail, a second magnet, a steel bolt and a steel spoon. The helper labels them A to E, so the tester does not know which is which.
flow.say: I have five pieces for you. Some are real magnets and some are only plain iron or steel. You can only use this hanging magnet. How could you tell which are the magnets?
flow.kid: A grown-up hides which pieces are magnets. You have one hanging magnet to test with. How could you tell which are the magnets?

ask.q: If a piece pulls the hanging magnet, is it a magnet?
good: Not for sure, because plain iron pulls too.
It could be a magnet or plain iron.
A pull could come from a magnet or from plain iron, so a pull proves nothing.

flow.parent: The point is to use a push as proof. Let your child say what they think first. If they say that a pull proves a magnet, let the test show them otherwise.
flow.context: This is the first step of the repel test. A helper hides which pieces are magnets.

flow.do: Take piece A. Bring one end near the hanging magnet, a few centimetres away. Does the magnet swing towards the piece or away from it? Write pull or push. Turn the piece round and test the other end. Do the same for B to E.
flow.say: Test both ends of each piece. Write pull or push for each end. If one end pushes the hanging magnet away, that piece is a real magnet.
flow.kid: Test both ends of each piece. Pull or push? Write it down.

check.q: A piece pulls the hanging magnet at one end and pushes it away at the other end. What is it?
options: A real magnet
Plain iron
A piece of wood
check.why: Only a magnet can push another magnet away. The push at one end shows that the piece has a pole of its own. Plain iron pulls at both ends, and wood does not move the magnet at all.

flow.parent: Hold each piece at the same distance and keep the tester still. A weak magnet may only push a little. A plain nail pulls at both ends. If a piece moves the hanging magnet at both ends in the same way, call it plain iron.
flow.context: In this step you test both ends of each piece with the hanging magnet.

flow.do: Sort the pieces into two piles, real magnets and plain iron. Write your verdict for each. Then the helper tells you which were magnets. Count how many verdicts were right.
flow.say: Make two piles. Which pieces pushed? Those are your magnets. Which only pulled? Those are plain iron. Now the helper tells you which were magnets. How many did you get right?
flow.kid: Make two piles. Magnets and plain iron. Now check. How many were right?
flow.think: A pull can fool you, and a push cannot. What other tests are good at saying no but not yes?
flow.parent: If a verdict was wrong, look at the notes together. A very weak magnet can look like plain iron. So the safest verdicts are 'one end pushed, so it is a magnet' and 'both ends only pulled, so it is probably plain iron'.
flow.context: In this step you sort the pieces and find out how many you got right.

flow.do: Swap places. Now your child prepares five mystery pieces for the parent, in secret, with letters A to E. The parent tests both ends with the hanging magnet and gives a verdict.
flow.say: Now you are the teacher. Hide which pieces are magnets, and let me test them. Then tell me if I got them right.
flow.kid: Now you hide the magnets. Let your parent test them. Were they right?
flow.parent: Let your child explain the push test back to you in their own words. This is the best way to find out what they have understood.
flow.context: In this last step your child sets the mystery pieces and checks the parent's verdicts.

activities.title: Two Faces of a Fridge Magnet: test both sides, then cut it in two

materials.item: a flat bendy fridge magnet, at least 5 cm by 5 cm, with a plain back
a plate with a heap of 30 small staples or tiny steel paper clips
a pair of scissors, used by a grown-up
a steel fridge door, almirah or tin tray
a pencil and paper
10 sheets of thin paper, to count how many the magnet holds on the fridge

schedule.what: Test the front and the back of the magnet on staples. A grown-up cuts it in two. Test the pieces. Slide the pieces over each other.

activities.record: A table: front, back, half 1 front, half 2 front, with the number of staples each held. Draw the cut magnet with the staples on it.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out why a fridge magnet grips on one face only, and what happens when you cut a magnet in two.

setup.art: A bendy fridge magnet face-down on a heap of staples with a few staples clinging, and its back face up.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the front face on the staples. Lift. Count the staples.

setup.art: The same magnet turned over with the back face on the staples and almost none clinging.
setup.caption: 2. Do the same with the back face. Count again.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting the magnet into two halves with scissors, with two halves side by side.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up cuts the magnet in two. Test each half.

flow.do: Find the front of the magnet, which is the side that grips the fridge. Ask your child to guess how many staples the front will pick up, and how many the back will pick up. Then lay the front on the heap of staples and lift it straight up. Count the staples.
flow.say: The front of this magnet sticks to the fridge. Will the back stick just as well? Guess how many staples each side will lift, and why.
flow.kid: Does the back stick as well as the front? Guess how many staples each lifts. Why?

ask.q: Do you think the two faces will hold the same number of staples?
good: Yes, it is one magnet.
No, the front is the part that sticks.
The front will hold more staples than the back.

flow.parent: A bendy magnet is weak, so it may lift only a few staples. That is fine. If it lifts none, try tiny paper clips or a pinch of steel wool, or press the magnet on the fridge and note how many sheets of paper it can hold.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Faces. You guess, then test the front face.

flow.do: Turn the magnet over and lay the back on the staples. Lift it and count. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.say: Now try the back. How many staples does it lift? Is it the same as the front?
flow.kid: Test the back face on the staples. Count them. Is it the same as the front?

check.q: The front of a bendy fridge magnet lifts many staples, and the back lifts almost none. What is the best explanation?
options: The magnet is made with stripes of north and south, so its field mostly reaches out of the front
The back is made of a different metal
The front is stronger because it is shinier
check.why: The maker magnetises the rubber in thin stripes of north and south. Their fields loop between neighbours and reach out of the front, and cancel at the back. Picking 'a different metal' mixes this up with the idea that a magnet must be a metal.

flow.context: In this step you test the back face and compare it with the front.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the magnet into two equal halves with scissors. Test the front of each half on the staples, and count. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Now a grown-up cuts the magnet in two. Is each half still a magnet? Is each half as strong as the whole? Test and see.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the magnet in two. Test each half on the staples. Is each half a magnet?

ask.q: Did you get one magnet and one piece of plain rubber?
good: No, both halves are magnets.
Each half has its own strong face.
Each half has its own north and south, so each half is a magnet.

flow.parent: Each half should still lift staples, usually about half as many as the whole, because it has half the area. Cut with sharp scissors by pulling the blade through the rubber in one go. Keep the small pieces away from children under five.
flow.context: In this step a grown-up cuts the magnet in two, and you test each half.

flow.do: Lay the two halves front to front and slide one over the other slowly. Notice what it feels like. Then press one half to the fridge and count how many sheets of paper it holds. Write what you found.
flow.say: Slide one half over the other, front to front. Do you feel any bumps or clicks? That feeling is the stripes lining up and slipping past each other.
flow.kid: Slide the two halves over each other. Do you feel little bumps?
flow.think: A magnet cut in two gives two magnets, each with its own two sides. What do you think would happen if you cut one of the halves in two again?
flow.parent: Not every magnet sheet feels bumpy, because the stripes can be very fine. If you feel nothing, write that down. It is still a true result. Some science museums have a magnetic viewing film that shows the stripes.
flow.context: In this last step you slide the halves over each other and press one on the fridge.

activities.title: Magnet Against the Earth: how many grams can your magnet hold?

materials.item: a strong magnet with a flat face, a ceramic disc or a neodymium magnet
a steel nail or a steel bolt, with a thread tied under its head
a small plastic cup with the thread tied to it
a bag of rice and a spoon
a kitchen scale, or a tablespoon to count spoonfuls
tape, to hold the magnet face down at the table edge, and a sheet of paper

schedule.what: Tape the magnet at the table edge. Hang the nail and the cup of rice from it. Add rice until the nail drops. Weigh the rice. Repeat with a sheet of paper between the nail and the magnet, and then with a thick bolt.

activities.record: A table with the grams of rice each time: nail touching the magnet, nail with one sheet of paper between, and a thick bolt touching the magnet.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out how much weight a magnet can hold against the pull of the whole Earth, and how it changes when there is paper in between.

setup.art: A magnet taped face down at the edge of a table with a nail stuck to its face and a thread running down to a plastic cup.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the magnet at the table edge. Stick the nail to its face. Hang the cup from the nail.

setup.art: A spoon dropping rice, a spoonful at a time, into the hanging cup until the nail comes off.
setup.caption: 2. Add rice, one spoonful at a time, until the nail falls.

setup.art: A kitchen scale showing the weight of the rice from the cup.
setup.caption: 3. Weigh the rice. That is how much the magnet held.

flow.do: Tape the magnet face down at the table edge, so its face overhangs. Stick the nail to its face. Tie the thread to the nail and hang the cup from the thread. Ask your child to guess how many grams of rice the magnet will hold, and why.
flow.say: The Earth is pulling this nail down. The magnet is pulling it up. How much rice can we put in the cup before the Earth wins? Make a guess, and give a reason.
flow.kid: The Earth pulls the nail down. The magnet pulls it up. How much rice can the cup hold? Guess.

ask.q: How many grams of rice do you think the cup can hold before the nail falls?
good: About 100 grams.
A lot, because the magnet is strong.
Hardly any.

flow.parent: A small ceramic magnet usually holds the nail and some rice, maybe 50 to 300 grams in all. A neodymium magnet may hold much more. Put a cushion on the floor below to catch the cup.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Magnet Against the Earth test. You guess, then build.

flow.do: Add rice to the cup, one spoonful at a time, slowly. Stop when the nail comes off the magnet. Weigh the cup with the rice, or count the spoonfuls. Repeat three times.
flow.say: Add a spoonful of rice. Wait. Add another. Keep going slowly. When the nail falls, we know the Earth's pull has beaten the magnet's pull. Write down the weight.
flow.kid: Add rice, a spoonful at a time. When the nail falls, stop. Weigh the rice.

check.q: The nail falls when the cup of rice is heavy enough. What does this mean?
options: The Earth's pull on the cup, nail and rice has become bigger than the magnet's pull
The magnet has run out of magnetism
The rice is magnetic
check.why: The magnet's pull stays the same. As rice is added, the weight, which is the Earth's pull, grows until it wins. Picking 'run out of magnetism' is wrong, because the magnet still works afterwards.

flow.parent: One level tablespoon of rice weighs about 10 to 15 grams, so counting spoonfuls gives a rough guess if you have no scale. The weight of the nail and cup counts too, but is small. Write down the biggest weight held, not the first drop.
flow.context: In this step you add rice until the Earth wins, and weigh the rice.

flow.do: Put one sheet of paper between the nail and the magnet. Repeat the test. Then use a thick bolt without paper. Write all three weights.
flow.say: Now a sheet of paper sits between the magnet and the nail. Does the magnet hold more or less? Then we try a thick bolt in place of the nail.
flow.kid: Put a sheet of paper between the magnet and the nail. Test again. Then try a thick bolt.

ask.q: Why might the magnet hold less when there is paper in between?
good: The paper keeps the nail further from the magnet, and the pull is weaker further away.
There is a small gap.
The pull of a magnet drops quickly with distance.

flow.parent: Expect the paper to cut the weight held a lot, because the pull falls quickly with distance. A thick bolt usually holds more than a thin nail, because there is more iron to magnetise.
flow.context: In this step you test with a paper gap and with a thick bolt.

flow.do: Write your three numbers. Ask your child which was biggest, which smallest, and why. Then ask what everyday thing weighs about as much as the magnet held, for example a few packets of biscuits.
flow.say: Which test held the most? Which held the least? What does this tell you about the magnet's pull?
flow.kid: Which held the most? Which held the least? Why?
flow.think: A tiny magnet beats the pull of a whole planet at a gap of a few millimetres. Why do you think it loses at a gap of a metre?
flow.context: In this last step you compare the three results and think about the pull of the magnet and the pull of the Earth.

activities.title: Hidden Magnets at Home: where are they, and how do you know?

materials.item: a steel paper clip, to test for any magnet or magnetic metal
a magnet on a thread, as a tester
a notebook and a pencil
a ruler, to measure how far the hanging magnet swings

schedule.what: Hunt for hidden magnets in the kitchen and the house. Test each find with a paper clip and a hanging magnet. List which are magnets and which are only magnetic.

activities.record: A list: where you looked, what the paper clip did, what the hanging magnet did, and your verdict: a magnet, or only magnetic.
activities.context: In this activity, you search your home for hidden magnets and use the repel test to tell real magnets from plain iron.

setup.art: A child holding a paper clip against a fridge door seal and a cupboard catch with a notebook open.
setup.caption: 1. Go round the home. Touch a paper clip to door seals, catches and speakers.

setup.art: A hanging magnet swinging away from a loudspeaker.
setup.caption: 2. Check with a hanging magnet. A push means a real magnet is hidden there.

setup.art: A child drawing a map of a home with stars where real magnets were found.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the real magnets on a map of your home.

flow.do: Make a list of places that may have magnets. Try the fridge door seal, cupboard catches, old earphones, a loudspeaker, a bag flap, a pencil box and a toy. Ask your child to guess which three have a real magnet.
flow.say: Many things at home have hidden magnets. Here is a list of places. Which three do you think have a real magnet in them? Why?
flow.kid: Where could magnets hide? Make a list. Which three have a real magnet?
flow.parent: Do not take things apart, because batteries and small parts are not safe to open. Only test from the outside. Keep the hanging magnet and paper clip away from phones, watches and bank cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Hidden Magnets hunt. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Visit each place on the list. Touch the paper clip to it. If the clip sticks or moves, hold the hanging magnet near and check for a push. Write what happens.
flow.say: Touch the paper clip first. If it sticks, there is a magnet or a magnetic metal inside. Then bring the hanging magnet close. If it gets pushed away at any point, there is a real magnet.
flow.kid: Touch a clip to each place. If it sticks, hold the hanging magnet near. Does it push?

check.q: The fridge door pulls a paper clip, but it does not push the hanging magnet away at any spot. What is the door?
options: Plain magnetic steel, which is not a magnet
A strong magnet
A plastic sheet
check.why: The door pulls both ends of the hanging magnet, so it is plain magnetic steel. A real magnet would push the hanging magnet away at one of its poles. A plastic sheet would not move the clip at all.

flow.parent: The rubber seal of the fridge door nearly always has a magnetic strip, so the clip clings and some spots may push the hanging magnet. Loudspeakers and old earphones often have strong ceramic or neodymium magnets inside.
flow.context: In this step you test each place with a paper clip and a hanging magnet.

flow.do: Make two lists: real magnets and plain magnetic metals. Count your finds. Pick the most surprising place and draw it.
flow.say: Which places had real magnets? Which had only plain magnetic metal? Which find surprised you most? Draw it.
flow.kid: Make two lists. Real magnets. Plain magnetic metal. Which surprised you most?
flow.think: A fridge door seal has a magnet inside, and nobody can see it. What other useful things are hidden inside everyday things?
flow.context: In this step you sort your finds into two lists and draw the most surprising one.

flow.do: Make a safety note. Write down which places must be kept away from bank cards, phones and watches, because they have strong magnets. Stick the note on the fridge.
flow.say: Strong magnets can scramble a bank card or a hotel key card. Which of our finds should we keep away from cards? Write it on a note.
flow.kid: Write a note. Which finds must stay away from cards and phones?
flow.parent: Magnets can wipe a magnetic stripe. Phones are less at risk than old cards, but a strong magnet near a phone's compass can confuse it.
flow.context: In this step you write a safety note about the strong magnets you found.

activities.title: Magnetic Memory: write your name in ups and downs

materials.item: a strip of card, 30 cm long, with 25 squares of 1 cm drawn along it
25 small arrows cut from paper, or 25 short pencil strokes
a pencil and paper
a friend or a parent to read the code back

schedule.what: Learn the up and down code. Write your first name in arrows. Swap strips with a friend and read each other's names.

activities.record: Your strip with the arrows, the letters written under it, and a note of how many arrows your name used.
activities.context: In this activity, you model how a hard disk or a magnetic stripe stores information, using arrows that point up or down like tiny magnetised regions.

setup.art: A strip of card with squares, each holding a small arrow pointing up or down.
setup.caption: 1. Each square holds one arrow. Up means 1. Down means 0.

setup.art: A table of letters A to E with five arrows for each, for example A is down down down down up.
setup.caption: 2. Each letter uses five arrows. A is 00001. B is 00010.

setup.art: Two friends swapping strips and reading the letters off.
setup.caption: 3. Swap strips with a friend. Read each other's names.

flow.do: Explain the code. Up is 1 and down is 0. Each letter uses five arrows. A is the number 1, B is 2, C is 3, and so on. Write each number as five 1s and 0s: 1 is 00001, 2 is 00010, 3 is 00011, 4 is 00100, 5 is 00101.
flow.say: A hard disk has millions of tiny regions. Each is magnetised up or down. We can use ups and downs to write letters. Each letter gets a number, and each number gets five ups and downs.
flow.kid: Up is 1. Down is 0. Each letter is five arrows. A is 00001. B is 00010.

ask.q: How would you write the letter D with five arrows?
good: D is the number 4, so 00100: down, down, up, down, down.
D is number 4, written 00100 with five arrows.
D is the fourth letter, so its number is 4.

flow.parent: Reading from the right, the places are worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. So 00101 is 4 plus 1, which is 5, the letter E. Help your child read a place at a time, from the right.
flow.context: This is the first step of Magnetic Memory. You learn the up and down code.

flow.do: Write your child's first name in the code. Look up each letter's number, turn it into five arrows, and lay the arrows along the strip. Leave one empty square between letters.
flow.say: Write your name in ups and downs. Find each letter's number. Turn it into five arrows. Put them along the strip.
flow.kid: Find each letter's number. Write it with five arrows. Lay them on the strip.

check.q: In the code, each arrow is up or down. What does an arrow stand for on a real hard disk?
options: A tiny region of magnetic material that points one way or the other
A tiny light that is on or off
A tiny letter printed on the disk
check.why: A hard disk stores information as millions of tiny regions of magnetic material, each magnetised one way or the other. Picking 'a tiny light' mixes up the disk with a screen.

flow.parent: The letters are numbered 1 to 26. Z, the 26th, is 11010. Take your time. The number for K is 11, which is 01011.
flow.context: In this step you write your name in arrows.

flow.do: Swap strips with a friend or a parent. Each reads the other's name from the arrows. Then ask the closing question.
flow.say: Swap strips. Read your friend's name from the arrows. Read five arrows at a time. Each five make one letter. What does it say?
flow.kid: Swap strips. Read the name. Five arrows make one letter.
flow.think: A real hard disk can only keep this pattern if its tiny magnetised regions stay put for years. What kind of magnetic material does that need, soft or hard?
flow.parent: The answer is hard. A soft material would let the pattern fade. This is why hard disks use hard magnetic coatings.
flow.context: In this step you swap strips, read each other's names and think about why the disk needs a hard magnetic material.

flow.do: Now mix up some arrows on a strip by flipping three of them. Ask a friend to read it. Talk about what happened to the name, and why a hard disk needs a hard magnetic material.
flow.say: If a few ups and downs flip by mistake, what happens to the name? Hard disks use hard magnetic materials so that this does not happen.
flow.kid: Flip three arrows on a strip. Read the name now. What went wrong?
flow.think: A soft material would let the arrows flip by themselves. How would a hard disk made of a soft material behave?
flow.context: In this step you flip some arrows to see why the pattern must stay put.

projects.title: Build a Magnetic Toy Train, then make it meet softly

materials.item: 2 or 3 small toy cars or matchbox-sized cardboard boxes on bottle-cap wheels, to be the engine and the carriages
2 small magnets, ceramic discs or neodymium, taped inside the engine
3 steel nails or big paper clips, taped inside each carriage
modelling clay, to balance the weights
tape, a smooth table and a ruler

projects.safety: Keep the small magnets and nails away from children under five. Do not let a magnet near phones, watches or bank cards.

schedule.what: Build the engine and a carriage. Test how far apart they can start and still join. Try the pair on a smooth table.
Balance the weights with clay. Try a weaker magnet. Make the join soft. Show the train to someone and say what you changed and why.

projects.record: Draw your train. Write the start gap, which car moved, how hard the cars met, and what you changed on day 2.
projects.context: In this project, you build a small magnetic train like the toy makers of Channapatna might. You make the carriages join without hooks, and you make the join gentle.

setup.art: A toy engine with a magnet taped inside its back and a toy carriage with nails taped inside its front, on a smooth table.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a magnet inside the engine and a nail inside the carriage.

setup.art: The engine and the carriage placed 5 centimetres apart on a table with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Place them 5 cm apart. Let go. Do they join?

setup.art: A lump of clay added to the lightest car, making the two cars equal.
setup.caption: 3. Add clay to the lighter car until both weigh the same.

flow.do: Show your child the cars, magnets and nails. Ask them to draw how to join two cars without a hook. Then ask which car will move when they are let go.
flow.say: We will make a train whose carriages join without hooks. We put a magnet in the engine and nails in the carriage. When we let go, which car do you think will move? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A magnet in the engine. A nail in the carriage. Which will move? Why?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If you have not done the Rafts experiment, do it first. It makes this project easier to explain.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Magnetic Toy Train. You plan before you build.

flow.do: Tape a magnet inside the back of the engine, with its flat face towards the back. Tape the nails inside the front of the carriage. Put them on a smooth table, 5 cm apart. Let go of both at once. Watch.
flow.say: Tape the magnet in the engine and the nails in the carriage. Put them 5 centimetres apart and let go. Which one moves? Do they both move?
flow.kid: Tape the magnet in the engine. Tape the nails in the carriage. Let go. Watch both cars.

check.q: The engine and the carriage both move towards each other. What does this show?
options: The magnet and the nail pull each other
The table is sloping
The magnet is pulling the nail only
check.why: Both cars moved, so both are pulled. If only the magnet pulled, only the nail car would move. A table that slopes would move both the same way, not towards each other.

flow.parent: If neither car moves, move them closer, or use a stronger magnet, or add a second nail. If they bang together hard, go on early to the day 2 step, where you make the join gentle.
flow.context: In this step you build the engine and the carriage and let go of both.

flow.do: Find the longest gap from which the cars still join. Move the cars apart 1 cm at a time. Write that gap. Then swap the roles, with the magnet in the carriage and the nails in the engine, and test again.
flow.say: How far apart can they start and still find each other? Move them back one centimetre at a time. Then swap, so the magnet is in the carriage. Does it change anything?
flow.kid: Move the cars apart 1 cm at a time. When do they stop joining? Swap the roles.
flow.parent: The gap is usually the same whichever car has the magnet. Pulls are always a pair.
flow.context: In this step you find the longest gap, and swap the magnet and the nails.

flow.do: On day 2, make the two cars weigh the same by adding clay to the lighter car. Use a weaker magnet or one nail fewer. Let go again. Aim for a soft click rather than a bang.
flow.say: Today we make the join gentle. Add clay to the lighter car so the two weigh the same. Then try a weaker magnet. We want the cars to meet softly, in the middle.
flow.kid: Add clay to the lighter car. Use a weaker magnet. Let go. Is the click softer?

ask.q: Why does a heavier car move less than a lighter car?
good: The same pull moves a light thing further.
A heavy thing is harder to get moving.
Pulling a heavy thing is like pushing a heavy school bag. It moves slowly.

flow.parent: A kitchen scale helps to weigh both cars. If you do not have one, hold the cars one in each hand and add clay until they feel equal.
flow.context: On day 2, you balance the weights and make the cars meet softly.

flow.do: Show the train to a friend or a grown-up. Ask your child to say what they changed and why, using the words pull, mass and equal.
flow.say: Show someone your train. Tell them what you changed on day 2, and why it made the meeting softer.
flow.kid: Show your train. Tell someone what you changed and why.
flow.think: In the story The Train That Met in the Middle, the engine twitched backwards when the carriage rushed forward. What does that tell you about the pull?
flow.context: In this last step you show the train and explain what you changed.

challenges.title: Lift the Heaviest Load with One Magnet
challenges.problem: You have one magnet, one steel nail or bolt, thread, a cup and rice. Find the way to arrange the steel so the magnet holds the most grams of rice before the steel falls.
constraints: You may use only one magnet. You may not tape the steel to the magnet.
You may use any of these steel things: a nail, a bolt, a spoon, a thin sheet of tin and a few paper clips.
Add the rice gently, one spoonful at a time.
Weigh the rice at the end, in grams.
materials: a magnet with a flat face
steel things: a nail, a bolt, a spoon, a tin sheet and paper clips
thread, a small plastic cup and rice
a kitchen scale or a tablespoon
general: Use a thick bolt rather than a thin nail, because it has more iron to magnetise.
Press the flat face of the steel firmly against the flat face of the magnet, with no gap.
Use two steel things stacked, so there is more iron close to the magnet.
creative: Put a thick flat steel washer on the face of the magnet and hang the load from the washer, so the washer spreads the pull.
Rub the surfaces smooth so that no tiny gaps remain, or use a drop of water to fill them.
Hang the load from the steel as low down as possible, so the load pulls the steel straight off and not sideways.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design and build it. Test it three times. Change one thing and test again. Which arrangement held the most rice? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the pull of a magnet. You find the best way to use one magnet to hold the heaviest load.

setup.art: A magnet at a table edge with a steel bolt stuck to its face and a cup hanging from the bolt.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a cup of rice from a bolt held by the magnet.

setup.art: A steel washer between the magnet and the bolt, with a thicker pull arrow.
setup.caption: 2. Try a washer or a stack of steel between the magnet and the load.

setup.art: A kitchen scale with the cup of rice on it.
setup.caption: 3. Weigh the rice in the cup, in grams.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the constraints. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs, and to say which they think will hold the most.
flow.say: You have one magnet. How can you arrange the steel so the magnet holds as much rice as possible? Draw some ideas first, and say which will win.
flow.kid: One magnet. How can you hold the most rice? Draw some ideas first.

ask.q: What would make the pull stronger?
good: More iron close to the magnet.
No gap between the steel and the magnet.
A thicker piece of steel.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Heaviest Load challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build your first design. Add rice until the steel falls. Weigh the rice. Write the number, which is the one to beat.
flow.say: Build your first design. Load it. How many grams does it hold? Write it down, so you have something to beat.
flow.kid: Build your first design. Add rice. Weigh it. Write the number.
flow.parent: Put a cushion under the cup. The steel often lets go with a sudden jerk, so add the last spoonfuls very slowly.
flow.context: In this step you build your first design and test it.

flow.do: Change one thing in your design, for example the thickness of the steel, and test again. Repeat with two more designs. Write all the numbers.
flow.say: Change just one thing, such as a thicker piece of steel. Test again. Is the number bigger? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Is the number bigger?

check.q: A thick bolt holds more rice than a thin nail on the same magnet. What is the best explanation?
options: A thick bolt has more iron with domains that can turn, so it makes a stronger induced magnet
A thick bolt is heavier so it sticks harder
A thick bolt is a different metal
check.why: A thin nail saturates early, because it has only a few domains to turn. A thick bolt has many more, so it becomes a stronger magnet itself. Picking 'heavier so it sticks harder' is the opposite of what happens, as a heavier thing is harder to hold up.

flow.context: In this step you improve your design and test again.

flow.do: Compare all your designs. Pick the winner, and write why you think it won, using the word saturated.
flow.say: Which design held the most? Why do you think it won? Use the word saturated if you can.
flow.kid: Which design held the most? Why do you think it won?
flow.think: A magnet can lift more with a thick bolt than with a thin nail. Where do you think the extra strength comes from?
flow.context: In this last step you compare your designs and explain the winner.

challenges.title: The Gentle Gate: a door catch that shuts itself and opens with one finger
challenges.problem: Make a small cardboard cupboard door that swings shut and is held closed by a magnet. It must stay shut if the cupboard is bumped, but a child must be able to open it with one finger.
constraints: Use cardboard for the door and the frame. Use tape for the hinge.
Use only magnets and steel that you already have.
The door must stay shut when you tap the table 5 times, and must open with one finger.
Keep magnets away from phones and bank cards.
materials: two sheets of cardboard and tape
a small flat magnet, or a piece of bendy fridge magnet
steel things: paper clips, a washer or a piece of tin
general: Tape a magnet to the edge of the frame and a steel washer to the edge of the door, so they touch when the door shuts.
Use a weak magnet, so a finger can open the door easily.
Make the door and the frame close with no gap.
creative: Use two bendy magnets with their stripes lined up, so the door clicks into one place only.
Put a thin sheet of paper between the magnet and the steel, to make the grip a little weaker.
Put a small magnet at the top and one at the bottom of the door, so it shuts straight and evenly.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your door. Build it. Tap the table 5 times and open it with one finger. Change the strength of the grip by changing the gap. Which gap gave a door that stays shut but opens easily? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about the strength of a magnet's pull and how it changes with a gap. You make a gentle door catch.

setup.art: A cardboard cupboard with a door taped on one side and a small magnet taped to the frame edge.
setup.caption: 1. Tape the door on one side. Tape the magnet to the frame.

setup.art: A steel washer taped to the door edge, meeting the magnet when the door shuts.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a steel washer to the door edge, where the magnet will meet it.

setup.art: A finger opening the closed door while another hand taps the table.
setup.caption: 3. Tap the table. Does the door stay shut? Open it with one finger.

flow.do: Read the problem. Ask your child to say what makes a good catch, and to draw the door, the frame, the magnet and the steel.
flow.say: We want a door that stays shut when the cupboard is bumped, but opens with one finger. What should the catch be like? Not too strong and not too weak. Draw your idea.
flow.kid: A door that stays shut but opens with one finger. Draw your idea.

ask.q: What could you change to make the catch weaker or stronger?
good: A weaker magnet.
A gap between the magnet and the steel.
More steel.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Gentle Gate challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Build the door and the frame. Tape the magnet to the frame and the steel to the door. Shut the door. Tap the table 5 times, and then open it with one finger.
flow.say: Build your door. Does it stay shut when you tap the table? Can you open it with one finger?
flow.kid: Build your door. Tap the table 5 times. Open it with one finger.
flow.parent: If the door will not stay shut, add a second magnet or a bigger washer. If it is too hard to open, add a layer of paper between the magnet and the steel.
flow.context: In this step you build your first door and test it.

flow.do: Change the grip by adding or taking away sheets of paper between the magnet and the steel. Test the door after each change. Write how many sheets of paper gave the best catch.
flow.say: Add one sheet of paper between the magnet and the steel. Test again. Then another. How many sheets give a catch that holds but opens easily?
flow.kid: Add a sheet of paper. Test the door. Add another. Which is best?

check.q: Adding paper between a magnet and the steel makes the catch weaker. Why?
options: The paper keeps the steel further away, and the pull gets weaker quickly with distance
The paper is a magnetic material
The paper makes the magnet colder
check.why: A magnet's pull is strongest close up and gets weaker quickly as the gap grows. Each sheet of paper adds to the gap. Picking 'the paper is magnetic' is wrong, because paper is not a magnetic material.

flow.context: In this step you change the gap and find the best catch.

flow.do: Show your door to someone. Ask your child to explain how it works, using the words magnet, steel, pull and gap.
flow.say: Show someone your door. Explain how it works. Use the words magnet, steel, pull and gap.
flow.kid: Show your door. Tell someone how it works.
flow.think: A good catch holds when it should and lets go when it should. What other things in life work like that?
flow.context: In this last step you show your door and explain how the catch works.

items.p: A magnet attracts a steel nail. Which sentence is true?
opts: The magnet and the nail pull each other equally
items.why: A pull always comes as a pair of equal forces, one on each thing. Picking 'only the magnet pulls' comes from watching the nail move, because the magnet is usually held in a hand.

items.p: A magnet sits on a light raft, and a nail sits on another raft of the same mass. They float 8 cm apart. What happens?
opts: Both rafts move towards each other and meet near the middle
items.why: The pulls are equal and the masses are equal, so both rafts move the same distance. Saying that only one raft moves forgets that the pull works both ways.

items.p: The same magnet pulls two rafts, but one raft is three times as heavy. Which statement is right?
opts: The heavy raft is pulled three times as hard
The light raft is pulled harder
The pulls are equal, so the light raft moves further
items.why: The pulls on both are equal. The same pull makes a light raft move faster and further than a heavy raft. The light raft is not pulled harder.

items.p: Two plain iron nails with no magnet near them pull each other strongly.
items.why: False. A plain nail is not a magnet, so it has no pull of its own. A nail only becomes a magnet when a magnet is near it.

items.p: A nail hanging from a magnet becomes a ____ magnet, because it only works while the magnet is near.
items.why: A temporary magnet works only while a magnet is near it. A permanent magnet keeps its magnetism by itself.

items.p: You have one magnet and a mystery piece of metal. How can you tell if the piece is a real magnet or only plain iron?
items.a: Hang the magnet on a thread. Bring one end of the piece near, then the other end. If either end pushes the magnet away, the piece is a real magnet. If both ends only pull, it is plain iron.
items.why: A strong answer says that a push is the proof, and a pull is not.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a piece of iron made into a magnet by a nearby magnet
a piece of soft iron laid across the poles of a stored magnet
keeps its magnetism for a long time
when all the domains already point the same way
items.why: These words describe how iron behaves near a magnet. A strong answer can give an example of each.

items.p: Sort each job: does the magnet in it need a hard material that keeps its magnetism, or a soft material that loses it?
items: the core of an electric bell
the core of a scrapyard crane magnet
the coating on a hard disk
items.why: A magnet that must last for years needs a hard material. A magnet that must switch off needs a soft one.

items.p: A sewing needle keeps its pins after the magnet is taken away. A plain nail drops most of its pins. What does this show?
opts: The needle is a harder magnetic material than the nail
The nail is a different metal
items.why: In hard steel the domains stay turned. In soft iron they turn back. Picking 'bigger' is a good guess, but the needle is thinner than the nail.

items.p: Three of these can be made into magnets by a magnet. Which one cannot?
items.why: Wood is not a magnetic material, so a magnet cannot turn it into a magnet. Iron and steel can be turned into magnets.

items.p: A friend says, 'The magnet is the only one pulling. The nail is just pulled.' What would you say to your friend? Use what you know about rafts.
items.a: If I float the magnet on a raft and hold the nail still, the magnet moves to the nail. So the nail is pulling the magnet. The two pulls are equal. The one that is free to move is the one you see move.
items.why: A strong answer says the pulls are equal and that the free thing is the one that moves.

items.p: You hang two nails from the same face of a magnet. Their tips spread apart. Why?
opts: The tips are the same kind of pole and repel
The tips are attracted to the table
items.why: Each nail becomes a magnet. Both heads touch the same pole, so both tips get the opposite pole. Two poles of the same kind repel.

items.p: A bendy fridge magnet grips just as well on its back as on its front.
items.why: False. The stripes of north and south are arranged so that the field reaches out of the front and cancels at the back. The front grips and the back hardly does.

items.p: Hammering a magnet hard many times makes it ____, because the knocks shake its domains out of line.
items.why: Knocks and heat both shake the domains. A strong opposite magnet can also weaken a magnet.

items.p: A small magnet can hold a nail up against the pull of the whole ____.
items.why: The Earth pulls the nail down, and the magnet wins at a short gap. Gravity is the weakest of the forces.

items.p: Draw a magnet with a nail hanging from it and a paper clip hanging from the nail. Draw small arrows inside the nail and the clip to show which way their tiny magnets point.
items.a: A magnet at the top, a nail below it and a clip below the nail. Inside the nail and the clip, small arrows all point the same way as the magnet's field.
items.why: The magnet turns the domains in the nail, and the nail turns the domains in the clip. All the small arrows point the same way.
items.art: A blank page with a bar magnet at the top.

items.p: Two girls of the same weight stand on roller skates and hold a rope between them. One pulls the rope. What happens?
opts: Only the girl who pulls moves
items.why: The rope pulls both girls with an equal force. So both slide towards each other. This is the same as the rafts, and it is Newton's third law.

items.p: A lighter girl on skates and a heavier woman on skates hold a rope and the girl pulls. Who moves further?
opts: The girl, because she is lighter
The woman, because she is stronger
items.why: The rope pulls both with the same force. The lighter person speeds up more and moves further. This is like the light raft and the heavy raft.

items.p: A strong neodymium magnet and a weak fridge magnet float on equal rafts. Which is pulled harder by the other?
opts: The weak magnet is pulled harder by the strong one
The strong magnet is pulled harder
Both are pulled with exactly the same force
items.why: There is only one pair of forces between the two magnets, equal in size. The strong magnet cannot pull harder than it is pulled. Picking the weak one is natural, but both rafts move the same.

items.p: Put these steps of the repel test in order.
items: Hang a known magnet on a thread and wait until it is still
Bring one end of the mystery piece near it and watch
Turn the piece round and test the other end
Decide: if either end pushed, it is a magnet
a: Hang a known magnet on a thread and wait until it is still
Bring one end of the mystery piece near it and watch
Turn the piece round and test the other end
Decide: if either end pushed, it is a magnet
items.why: You need a still tester first, then you test one end, then the other end, and only then decide. Testing one end is not enough, because a piece might pull at one end and push at the other.

items.p: A mystery piece pulls a hanging magnet at both ends. What is the safest verdict?
opts: It is plain magnetic metal, or a very weak magnet
It is a piece of wood
items.why: Plain iron pulls at both ends. A very weak magnet may not push enough to notice. Only a push proves a magnet, so 'plain magnetic metal' is the safest verdict.

items.p: Explain why steel for a permanent magnet needs to be hard and iron for the core of an electromagnet needs to be soft.
items.a: A permanent magnet must keep its magnetism for years, so it is made of a hard material whose domains stay turned. The core of an electromagnet must lose its magnetism as soon as the electricity is switched off, so it is made of soft iron whose domains turn back.
items.why: A strong answer connects hard with keeping and soft with letting go, and names the job each one does.

items.p: In pure soft iron, the edges of the domains slide about easily. In hard steel they catch on tiny bits of carbon. Which fits this idea?
opts: Hard steel keeps its magnetism, because its domain edges are held in place
Hard steel loses its magnetism, because its domain edges are free
Soft iron keeps its magnetism for years
items.why: Flaws and carbon in the steel hold the domain edges after they have turned. Soft iron lets the edges slide back at once.

items.p: Sort each thing: does it attract pins like a magnet, or paper scraps like a rubbed comb?
items: a plastic comb rubbed on dry hair
items.why: A magnet picks up iron and steel. A rubbed plastic comb or balloon picks up light scraps by static electricity. They are two sides of one force, but they behave differently.

items.p: Why is a thick bolt able to hold more weight than a thin nail on the same magnet?
opts: It has more iron, so it becomes a stronger induced magnet before it saturates
items.why: A thin nail has only so many domains to turn, and it saturates early. A thick bolt has many more domains. Picking 'heavier' is wrong, because heavier things are harder to hold up.

items.p: Storing a bar magnet loose in a drawer with steel tools always keeps it as strong as it was.
items.why: False. Steel tools can pull on the magnet's field and may slowly change it. Magnets are better stored in pairs with their poles reversed and an iron keeper at each end.

items.p: Two sisters see a fridge magnet stick to the fridge. They argue about who is pulling.

views.says: The magnet is pulling the fridge door. The door is too big to move, so it is only being pulled.
The door is pulling the magnet just as hard. We only see the magnet move because the door is too heavy to move.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Say how you could test it with rafts, and say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: The younger sister is right that the pulls are equal. The older sister is right that only the magnet moves, because the door is too heavy. A test is to float the magnet on a raft and hold a nail still. The magnet moves, which shows the nail pulls.
items.why: A strong answer says the pulls are equal and uses the raft test as evidence. It also says that the older sister is right about what we see.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a hard disk. Label three parts: the spinning plate, the tiny magnetised regions and the read head.
labels: Flat round plate coated with magnetic material
Tiny areas pointing up or down
Small arm that passes over the plate
items.art: A drawing of a spinning hard disk plate with tiny up and down arrows along a track and a thin arm above it.
a: Flat round plate coated with magnetic material: spinning plate
Tiny areas pointing up or down: tiny magnetised regions
Small arm that passes over the plate: read head
items.why: The regions hold the information, the plate holds the regions and the head reads or writes them.

items.p: A key card's stripe keeps its data for months because it is made of a ____ magnetic material.
items.why: A stripe must keep its pattern of ups and downs. That needs a hard magnetic material.

items.p: A fridge magnet's field reaches out of its ____ face and cancels at the back.
items.why: The thin north and south stripes in the rubber make loops that reach out of the front.

items.p: Draw two nails hanging from one magnet in a V. Mark the pole at each head and at each tip, using N and S.
items.a: A magnet at the top. Two nails hang below it in a V. If the magnet's pole at the heads is N, each head is S and each tip is N.
items.why: Both heads get the same pole, so both tips get the opposite pole. Two tips with the same pole repel.
items.art: A blank page with a flat magnet face at the top.

items.p: Three of these hold information by tiny regions magnetised up or down. Which one does not?
items.why: A printed page stores information as ink on paper, with no magnetic regions.

items.p: A hard disk keeps a song for years, but a soft iron core would forget it in a moment. Explain why in your own words.
items.a: A hard disk is coated with a hard magnetic material, which keeps its tiny regions turned the same way for years. A soft material would let them turn back, and the pattern would fade.
items.why: A strong answer connects hard with keeping the pattern, and soft with losing it.

items.p: A girl on roller skates pushes a wall and rolls backwards. Why?
opts: The wall pushes back on her with an equal force
items.why: When she pushes the wall, the wall pushes her. This is Newton's third law. She moves because she is free to roll and the wall is part of a building.

items.p: An apple falls from a tree. The Earth pulls the apple. Does the apple pull the Earth?
opts: Yes, with the same force, but the Earth moves by a tiny amount
No, the apple is too small
Yes, with a much bigger force
items.why: The pulls are equal in size. The Earth has so much mass that the same pull moves it by an amount nobody can see.

items.p: If a magnet and a nail are both held tightly in your hands, nothing is pulling.
items.why: False. The pulls are still there. Each hand feels the pull even though neither thing moves.

items.p: A comb rubbed on hair picks up a scrap of paper. A friend says, 'The comb is now a magnet.' How could you test it?
opts: See if the comb also picks up a steel pin
Look at the comb through a lens
items.why: A magnet picks up pins. A rubbed comb picks up paper but not pins. If the comb does not pick up the pin, it is static electricity and not magnetism.

items.p: Newton said it seemed absurd that one body could pull another across empty space. Faraday thought of lines of force filling the space. Why might a picture help scientists even if nobody can touch it?
items.a: A picture of lines or a field gives a way to think about where a pull acts and how strong it is at each place. Iron filings and compasses show the shape of it, and the picture lets us predict what a magnet will do.
items.why: A strong answer says that the picture lets us predict and test, and that this is useful whether or not the field is a thing.

items.p: Match each word to the idea it names.
pairs: when one thing pulls another, the other pulls back equally
domains in iron flip in sudden small jumps that can be heard
helps a stored magnet stay strong
all the domains in the iron already point the same way
items.why: Each word names an idea from the unit. A strong answer can give an example of each.

items.p: You find a long steel rod that picks up pins at one end only. It does not pull pins in the middle. What is the best conclusion?
opts: It is a magnet with a pole at that end
items.why: A magnet's pull is strongest at its poles. A plain rod pulls the same near any part.

items.p: Two friends disagree about whether a magnetic field is real.

views.says: The field is real. Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields, and it crosses empty space.
A field is only a map. We never measure the field itself, only the pull on a nail or a compass.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give one reason from the lessons. Then say what each friend would want to test next.
items.a: Either can be argued. The first friend has the evidence that light is a wave of fields and that fields carry energy. The second friend is right that we measure the effects on things. A strong answer gives evidence and says that scientists argue about the exact nature of a field.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence, names a limit of each view, and says what to test next.

items.p: A steel crane in a scrapyard uses a magnet to lift a car, then drops it. Which is the best core for this magnet?
opts: Soft iron, so it loses magnetism when the current stops
Hard steel, so it keeps its magnetism
items.why: Soft iron is a strong magnet while the current flows and stops being one when the current stops, so the crane can let go.

items.p: A magnet's pull gets weaker quickly as the ____ between it and the iron gets bigger.
items.why: A magnet's pull is strongest close up. It is much weaker a few centimetres away.

items.p: A piece of soft iron laid across the poles of a stored magnet is called a ____.
items.why: A keeper gives the field an easy loop and helps the magnet stay strong.

items.p: A needle stays magnetised for a month and a nail forgets in a minute. Describe what the 'memory' of the needle is, without using the word 'remember'.
items.a: In the needle, the domains stay turned the same way after the magnet has gone, because their edges are held in place. In the nail, the domains turn back.
items.why: A strong answer says what stays different inside the needle: the direction of its domains.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a bendy fridge magnet seen from the side. Label the front face, the back face and a pair of neighbouring stripes.
labels: A north stripe next to a south stripe
items.art: A side view of a thin magnet sheet with alternating north and south stripes and field loops coming out of one face only.
a: Face with fields reaching out: front face
Face with fields cancelling: back face
A north stripe next to a south stripe: neighbouring stripes
items.why: The loops between neighbouring stripes reach out of the front and cancel at the back.

items.p: You hang two long nails and two short nails from a magnet. The long ones spread more at the tips. What is the best explanation?
opts: The tips of long nails are further from the magnet and can move further apart
items.why: The two tips push each other apart, and long nails hang with the tips further out. Heavier nails would just hang straight down.

items.p: A magnet cut in half gives one piece with a north pole only and one piece with a south pole only.
items.why: False. Each piece is a magnet with its own north and south. Nobody has ever found a magnet with only one pole.

items.p: Draw two rafts, one with a magnet and one with a nail, at the start and after they have met. Show with arrows how far each raft moved when the nail raft is three times heavier.
items.a: At the start, the rafts are 8 cm apart, with equal pull arrows between them. After they meet, the magnet raft has moved about 6 cm and the heavy nail raft about 2 cm.
items.why: The pulls are equal but the lighter raft moves further. If the nail raft has three times the mass, the magnet raft moves about three times as far.
items.art: A blank drawing of a tub of water seen from above.

items.p: A friend says that a bendy fridge magnet is ruined if you cut it in two. What would you say?
items.a: Each half is still a magnet, because the stripes of north and south are all through the rubber. Each half is weaker, as it has half the area, but it still grips on its front face.
items.why: A strong answer says that every piece of a magnet has its own poles.

quiz.p: A magnet attracts a nail. What does the nail do to the magnet?
opts: Attracts it with an equal force
Attracts it with a smaller force
quiz.why: Pulls always come in pairs of equal size. The nail seems to do nothing because the magnet is usually held in a hand.

quiz.p: Two rafts of equal mass carry a magnet and a nail. Where do they meet?
quiz.why: The pulls are equal and the masses are equal, so both move the same distance and meet in the middle.

quiz.p: The same pull acts on a light thing and a heavy thing. Which moves further?
quiz.why: A pull makes a light thing speed up more than a heavy thing, so the light thing moves further.

quiz.p: A steel nail near a magnet picks up a pin. What has happened to the nail?
opts: It has become a magnet for as long as the magnet is near
It has become a different metal
quiz.why: The magnet turns the domains in the nail to point one way. The nail is now an induced magnet.

quiz.p: Two pins hang from one pole of a magnet. Their tips spread apart. Why?
opts: Both tips are the same pole, so they repel
quiz.why: Both pins become magnets with the same pole at their tips. Two poles of the same kind repel.

quiz.p: A mystery metal piece pushes a hanging magnet away at one end. What is the piece?
quiz.why: Only a magnet can push another magnet away.

quiz.p: A mystery piece pulls the hanging magnet at both ends and never pushes. What is it most likely?
quiz.why: A plain magnetic piece pulls at both ends. A plastic spoon or rubber band would not move the magnet at all.

quiz.p: A steel needle keeps its pins for days. A plain nail drops its pins in minutes. Which is the harder magnetic material?
quiz.why: In the needle the domains stay turned. In the nail they turn back.

quiz.p: What should the core of an electromagnet in a crane be made of?
quiz.why: Soft iron loses its magnetism when the current stops, so the crane can drop its load.

opts: Heating it, hammering it, or putting a strong opposite magnet near it
Holding a nail for a long time
Keeping it in a dry box
quiz.why: Heat, hard knocks and strong opposite fields shake the domains. Holding a nail takes nothing from a magnet.

quiz.p: Why are some bar magnets stored with an iron keeper across their poles?
opts: It gives the field an easy loop, which helps the magnet stay strong
It makes the pull stronger on the table
quiz.why: A keeper closes the loop of the field. This stops the magnet's own poles from turning its domains backwards.

quiz.p: A bendy fridge magnet grips on its front and hardly on its back. What is the reason?
opts: Thin stripes of north and south make the field reach out of the front only
The back is made of rubber and the front of steel
The front is a bigger magnet
quiz.why: The maker magnetises thin stripes side by side. The loops between neighbours reach out of one face and cancel at the other.

quiz.p: A hard disk stores information as tiny regions magnetised up or down. Why must the coating be a hard magnetic material?
opts: So the pattern stays for years
quiz.why: A soft material would let the pattern fade. A hard material keeps the domains turned.

quiz.p: A rubbed comb picks up paper scraps but not a steel pin. What does that show?
opts: The comb's pull is static electricity and not magnetism
The comb is a strong magnet
quiz.why: A magnet picks up pins. The comb does not, so its pull is a different one.

quiz.p: Scientists agree that a magnetic field works as a description of the pull around a magnet. What do they still argue about?
quiz.why: It is well tested that magnets attract iron, that nails can be magnetised and that pulls come in pairs. What a field is, underneath, is still being discussed.

applications: Scrapyard cranes with electromagnets lift cars and steel, and drop them when the electricity is switched off.
Electric bells, relays and door locks use a soft iron core that is a magnet only while current flows.
Cupboard catches and fridge door seals use permanent magnets that pull a door shut and let go when a finger pulls the door open.
Hard disks, cassette tapes and old bank cards store information in tiny magnetised regions of hard magnetic material.
Loudspeakers and earphones use a permanent magnet and a coil of wire to turn electricity into sound.
Electric fans, mixers and washing machines have motors with soft iron cores and permanent magnets.
Transformers use thin sheets of soft iron to carry the changing magnetic field from one coil to another.
Engineers listen to the crackle of magnetised steel to check whether a steel part was heated properly.
Magnetic locks on shop doors hold a door shut with an electromagnet and open when the current stops.
Magnetic separators in recycling plants and flour mills pull iron out of mixed waste and food.
Magnetic levitation trains float on a cushion of magnetic force, with an equal and opposite force on the track.

open_questions.q: What is a magnetic field, underneath?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can describe a magnetic field very well, and light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields. Whether a field is a thing in its own right or only a very good description is still argued.

open_questions.q: Why is gravity so much weaker than the magnetic force?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists have measured the difference, but nobody yet knows why the forces have the strengths that they do.

open_questions.q: Can we make a very strong magnet from common, cheap elements?
open_questions.why_open: The strongest magnets use rare earth metals, which are hard to dig and separate. Scientists are looking for new materials that do not need them.

open_questions.q: How exactly do the edges of domains move when a magnet is brought near?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see domain edges with special microscopes. Predicting how every flip happens in a real, messy piece of steel is still hard.

open_questions.q: Is there a limit to how much information a magnetic disk can hold?
open_questions.why_open: The tiny regions cannot be made too small or heat makes them flip. Engineers keep finding new tricks, and nobody is sure where the limit lies.

open_questions.q: Why do pulls come in pairs at all?
open_questions.why_open: The rule about pairs of forces has never failed in a test. Physics describes the rule, but it does not say why nature is built this way.

jokes.j: Why was the soft iron nail a bad secret keeper?
jokes.a: It could not hold on to anything for long.

jokes.j: Why was the steel needle such a good friend?

jokes.a: It was good at picking things up, and even better at letting go.

jokes.j: What do you call two nails that hang in a V?

jokes.a: It only had eyes for the front of the fridge.

jokes.j: What did the heavy raft say to the light raft?
jokes.a: You do all the running, and I do all the thinking.

jokes.j: Why did the bar magnet go to the party with an iron keeper?
jokes.a: It did not want to lose its attraction.

maths.problem: The magnet raft and the nail raft start 8 centimetres apart. The nail raft is three times as heavy. The lighter raft moves 3 times as far as the heavier one. How far does each raft move before they meet?
maths.answer: The magnet raft moves 6 centimetres. The heavy raft moves 2 centimetres.
maths.explain: Together they must cover 8 centimetres. The light raft moves 3 parts and the heavy raft moves 1 part, so there are 4 parts. 8 divided by 4 is 2 centimetres a part. The heavy raft moves 1 part, which is 2 centimetres. The light raft moves 3 parts, which is 6 centimetres. 6 plus 2 is 8, which checks.
maths.context: In the Rafts experiment, a magnet raft and a nail raft are 8 centimetres apart and pull each other with equal force.
maths.why_maths: A ratio tells you how a shared distance is split. It lets you predict the result before the rafts move.

maths.problem: A magnet held 240 grams of rice. With one sheet of paper between the magnet and the nail it held 80 grams. How many times as much did it hold with no paper?
maths.explain: 240 divided by 80 is 3. So the magnet held 3 times as much with no paper. Check: 80 plus 80 plus 80 is 240.
maths.context: In the Magnet Against the Earth activity, you add rice to a cup until the Earth's pull beats the magnet's pull.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one number by another tells us how many times bigger it is. A sentence like 'much weaker' becomes a number we can compare.

maths.problem: After stroking, a needle held 6 staples. The next day it held 5. What fraction of its staples did it still hold? And what fraction had it lost?
maths.answer: It still held five sixths and had lost one sixth.
maths.explain: It started with 6 staples. 5 out of 6 is five sixths. It lost 1 out of 6, which is one sixth. Five sixths plus one sixth makes one whole.
maths.context: In the Soft or Hard test, you count how many staples a needle can lift right after stroking, and again the next day.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells us how much of the magnetism was kept. Comparing fractions lets us compare the needle with the nail fairly.

maths.problem: The nail held 9 staples right after stroking, and 2 the next day. The needle held 6, then 5. Which one lost a bigger fraction of its staples?
maths.answer: The nail lost a bigger fraction.
maths.explain: The nail lost 7 out of 9, which is more than three quarters. The needle lost 1 out of 6, which is less than a fifth. So the nail lost a much bigger fraction, even though it started with more staples.
maths.context: In the Soft or Hard test, the nail starts strong but the needle keeps its staples.
maths.why_maths: The nail started with more staples. Only comparing the fractions each one lost shows which was really better at keeping its magnetism.

maths.problem: In the code for the magnetic memory, each letter is a number from 1 to 26, written with five arrows. Up is 1 and down is 0. The places are worth 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. M is the 13th letter. Write 13 with five arrows, using U for up and D for down.
maths.explain: 13 is 8 plus 4 plus 1. So the 8 place, the 4 place and the 1 place are up, and the 16 place and the 2 place are down. In order, the arrows are down, up, up, down, up. That is 01101.
maths.context: In the Magnetic Memory activity, you write letters with up and down arrows, like the tiny magnetised regions on a hard disk.
maths.why_maths: Place value is how a long row of ups and downs can stand for a number. This is how a disk stores letters.

maths.problem: A toy maker makes 200 magnetic trains. Each train needs 1 small magnet that costs 6 rupees and 3 steel nails that cost 1 rupee each. How much does she spend on magnets and nails for all 200 trains?
maths.explain: One train needs 6 rupees for the magnet and 3 rupees for the nails, which is 9 rupees. 200 trains cost 200 times 9. 200 times 9 is 1,800 rupees.
maths.context: In the Magnetic Toy Train project, you plan a train with a magnet in the engine and nails in the carriages.
maths.why_maths: A maker needs to know the cost of making many things from the cost of making one. Working out one first and multiplying is how it is done.

maths.problem: Suppose nails 2 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm long gave tip gaps of 0.5 cm, 1 cm and 1.5 cm. If the pattern continued, what tip gap would a 10 cm nail give? Why might a real nail give less?
maths.answer: 2.5 centimetres. A real nail may give less because the pull between the tips gets weaker with distance, and the nail's own weight pulls the tips down.
maths.explain: The gap grows by 0.5 cm for every 2 cm of nail. 10 cm is 5 steps of 2 cm, so the gap is 5 times 0.5, which is 2.5 cm. Real patterns often flatten out as the numbers get bigger.
maths.context: In the Hanging V experiment, you measure the gap between the tips of two nails that hang from one magnet.
maths.why_maths: Finding a pattern lets you guess a result that you have not measured. Then you can test whether the real world follows the pattern.

maths.problem: Look at the kitchen scale. It shows the weight of the cup of rice and the nail that a magnet held just before it let go. The pointer is halfway between the 200 gram mark and the 250 gram mark. How many grams is that?
maths.explain: Halfway between 200 and 250 is 200 plus half of 50. Half of 50 is 25. 200 plus 25 is 225 grams. The weight is the Earth's pull on the cup, nail and rice.
maths.context: In the Magnet Against the Earth activity, you weigh the cup of rice that a magnet just manages to hold.
maths.why_maths: A scale is only useful if you can read the place between two marks. That turns 'about 200' into an exact weight.

maths.problem: The first train used a magnet that made the carriage rush from 5 cm away. The second used a weaker magnet that started to pull only from 3 cm away. How many centimetres closer must the carriage start with the weaker magnet?
maths.explain: 5 take away 3 is 2. The carriage must start 2 centimetres closer with the weaker magnet.
maths.context: In the Magnetic Toy Train project, you change the magnet and find the longest gap from which the cars still join.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two gaps tells you how much a weaker magnet changes the design.
