roots.context: We have floated a magnet and a nail on rafts, hung two nails from a magnet in a V, and tested whether a needle or a nail keeps its magnetism longer. On the rafts, the nail pulled the magnet as hard as the magnet pulled the nail. Here we ask what that says about us and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A magnet and a nail pull each other with equal force. In the Rafts on the Water experiment, both rafts move. A pull is never one thing acting alone. It always takes two things, and each pulls the other.
deep_truth.habit: We say the magnet pulls the nail, as if the magnet acts and the nail is only acted on. We think this because we watch which one moves. The forces themselves are equal on both.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Rafts on the Water experiment, a magnet raft and a nail raft of equal mass meet in the middle. When the nail raft is made heavier, the pulls stay equal and the light raft travels further. The heavy raft still creeps a little, which shows that it is being pulled too.

three.who_am_i: When you push a wall, the wall pushes you. You cannot push or pull anything without being pushed or pulled back.
three.what_is_life: A root pushes into the soil, and the soil pushes back. A bird pushes air down, and the air lifts her up.
three.what_is_this_world: Every push and pull in the world comes as a pair. No force has ever been found alone.

roots.thread: A magnet and a nail look like two separate things, one doing and one being done to. But the pull between them is one pull with two ends. Take away either the magnet or the nail and the pull is gone. The same is true of every push and pull: it always joins two things. So the things in the world are not as separate as they look. Each one is joined to others by the pushes and pulls between them.

teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna, an Indian Buddhist teacher of about the 2nd century CE, taught that a doer and a deed depend on each other. There is no doer without a deed, and no deed without a doer.
teachings.link: A magnet is a puller only because there is a nail to pull. The pull is what they do together.

teachings.teaching: Being and non-being give birth to each other. Hard and easy complete each other. Long and short measure each other. Front and back follow each other.
teachings.link: A magnet always has a north pole and a south pole together. A pull has two ends, and each end needs the other.

teachings.source: Heraclitus, fragment B51 (Diels-Kranz numbering), about 500 BCE
teachings.teaching: Heraclitus said that the harmony of the world comes from tension that pulls in both directions, like the bow and the lyre.
teachings.link: A pulled bowstring pulls the bow back as hard as the bow pulls the string. Magnet and nail are held in the same kind of tension.

science.text: Newton's third law: when one body pulls on another, the second pulls on the first with an equal force in the opposite direction. It has never failed a test.
What a magnetic field is, underneath, and whether it is a thing or only a very good description.

other_view.view: Saying that forces come in pairs is a way of keeping accounts. It does not show that the world is joined together. In daily life, saying that a magnet pulls a nail is perfectly correct, and nothing needs to change in how we talk.

how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, many writers described the lodestone, the old magnet stone, as the active one that drew the iron, and the iron as the one that was only drawn. In 1600, the English doctor William Gilbert wrote that the attraction goes both ways. He reported floating a lodestone on the water in a small vessel and bringing iron near it, and the lodestone moved towards the iron. In 1687, Isaac Newton wrote down a rule for every push and pull in nature. When one body pushes or pulls another, the other pushes or pulls back with equal force in the opposite direction. The rule has been tested for more than three hundred years, on planets, on rockets and on magnets on rafts. It has never failed once.
how_we_found_out.who: William Gilbert, an English doctor, and Isaac Newton, an English mathematician
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many people thought the lodestone was the only one that pulled, and the iron was merely drawn. Gilbert's floating lodestone showed that the iron draws the lodestone too, and Newton showed that this is true of every pull.
